# 4-Week Postpartum On-Ramp Block
### Client Profile Recap
10 weeks postpartum | OB-cleared for moderate exercise | No jumping/high-impact until 14 weeks postpartum (i.e., after Week 4 of this block) | Training environment: home | Equipment: light dumbbells

---

## Overarching Design Principles

Before diving into the week-by-week detail, it is worth naming the philosophy driving every decision in this block, so you can explain the rationale to your client and adjust intelligently if her response to training varies.

**Intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) management remains the priority.** Her core is still in a healing state. Linea alba integrity, pelvic floor load tolerance, and the relationship between breath and bracing must be re-established before any meaningful external load is added. Every exercise is chosen or modified with IAP in mind.

**Symptoms are the compass.** She should be monitoring for leaking (urine or wind), heaviness or pressure in the pelvic floor, coning or doming at the midline, and pain. Any of these during or after a session is a signal to regress, not push through. Brief her on this before Week 1 begins.

**Sleep and hormonal context matter.** Relaxin is still elevated while she is breastfeeding (if she is), joints are lax, and fatigue is non-linear. Programme volume is deliberately low. Adaptation will come from consistency and quality, not from accumulation.

**Progression logic across the block:** Week 1 is a movement audit and nervous system re-introduction. Week 2 introduces structured loading at low volume. Week 3 adds a third session and begins building volume. Week 4 consolidates and tests readiness for the next phase.

---

## Equipment Assumed
- One pair of light dumbbells (suggest 2–4 kg to start; she will tell you quickly if these feel trivial or too heavy)
- A resistance band (loop or long) if available — useful but not essential
- A mat
- A sturdy chair or low step for support

---

---

# WEEK 1 — Acclimatisation

**Goal:** Reconnect with her body, establish breathing mechanics, assess movement quality, and build the habit of training without creating any symptom response. There is no performance target this week. You are gathering information.

**Sessions:** 3 sessions across the week, each 20–25 minutes. These are not workouts in the traditional sense — they are movement conversations.

**Session structure for all three sessions this week:**

Each session follows the same loose template: breathwork and pelvic floor check-in, a short movement sequence, and a brief cool-down with body awareness cues. The exercises are identical across all three sessions intentionally. Repetition at this stage builds motor pattern confidence, not boredom.

---

### Session Template (Weeks 1 — all three sessions)

**Opening: Diaphragmatic Breath and Pelvic Floor Re-connection — 5 minutes**

Have her lie in a comfortable semi-supine position (knees bent, feet flat). Ask her to place one hand on her lower ribcage and one on her lower abdomen. The cue is to breathe into the hands — ribcage expands three-dimensionally on the inhale, softens on the exhale. On the exhale, she should feel a gentle, natural lift and squeeze of the pelvic floor — not a forced Kegel, but a response to the breath. Spend 8–10 breath cycles here. This is also her daily homework: 5 minutes of this breathing every morning, separate from training sessions.

**Movement Sequence — 15 minutes**

*1. 90/90 Hip Lift — 2 sets of 5 breaths*
Lying supine, feet on a wall or chair at 90 degrees at hip and knee. On the exhale, gently posteriorly tilt the pelvis and feel the lower back connect lightly to the floor. Hold for a breath cycle, release. This resets lumbopelvic position and begins to re-engage the deep stabilisers without any load.

*2. Glute Bridge — 2 sets of 8 reps*
From the same supine position, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Inhale to prepare, exhale and drive through the heels to lift the hips. The cue is to think about lengthening the front of the hips rather than squeezing the glutes aggressively. Hold one second at the top, lower with control. Watch for any rib flare or breath-holding at the top. If she reports pelvic floor heaviness, reduce range of motion.

*3. Clam Shell — 2 sets of 10 reps each side*
Side-lying, hips stacked, knees bent to approximately 45 degrees. Keeping the feet together, rotate the top knee toward the ceiling. The pelvis must not rock backward — this is the coaching point. Slow and controlled. This begins to re-load the hip external rotators and glute medius without any spinal compression.

*4. Cat-Cow — 2 sets of 6 reps*
On all fours, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips. Move slowly through spinal flexion and extension, breathing continuously. Watch for any breath-holding or bracing. The purpose here is spinal mobility and body awareness, not strength.

*5. Wall Push-Up — 2 sets of 8 reps*
Standing facing a wall, hands at shoulder height and width. Inhale as she lowers toward the wall, exhale as she pushes away. Watch the midline — any coning or doming means she is generating too much IAP and needs to modify the breath strategy or reduce range. This is the first upper body load of the block and the first time you will see how her core responds to a pressing pattern.

*6. Supported Squat (Chair Squat) — 2 sets of 8 reps*
Standing in front of a sturdy chair, feet hip-to-shoulder width. She lowers slowly toward the chair — touching it lightly or hovering just above — then stands. Exhale on the way up. The chair removes the fear of depth and gives her a target. Watch for knee cave, forward trunk lean, and any pelvic floor symptoms on the way up from the bottom position.

**Cool-Down and Body Awareness — 3–5 minutes**

Child's pose (modified if tender at the knees — she can use a pillow under the hips), followed by a supine figure-four stretch for the hips. End with 2 minutes back in the semi-supine breathing position. Ask her to do a brief mental scan: any leaking, heaviness, or discomfort during the session? Any coning she noticed? This is data for you.

---

### Week 1 Homework (Daily, Outside Sessions)
- 5 minutes diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor connection, morning
- A 15–20 minute walk on non-session days, building to 30 minutes by end of the week if energy allows
- Hydration: minimum 2 litres of water daily, more if breastfeeding

### What You Are Assessing This Week
By the end of Week 1 you want to know: Can she coordinate breath with movement? Does she show any symptoms during the bridge, squat, or push-up? How is her hip mobility and glute activation quality? Is she fatigued after 20 minutes or does she have more in the tank? The answers to these questions will determine how aggressively you load Week 2.

---

---

# WEEK 2 — Foundation Loading

**Goal:** Introduce structured resistance training at low volume. Begin building the squat, hinge, push, and carry patterns that will underpin the next phase. Maintain symptom-free training as the non-negotiable standard.

**Sessions:** 3 sessions | 30–35 minutes each | Full body each session

**Session structure:** 5-minute breathing warm-up (same as Week 1), main block, 5-minute cool-down.

---

### Session A (repeat on Day 1 and Day 5)

**1. Glute Bridge with Dumbbell Hip Load — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Place one light dumbbell across the hip crease. Same mechanics as Week 1 but now with external load. The weight should feel noticeable but not cause any change in breathing pattern or symptom response. If it does, remove the dumbbell and continue unloaded.

**2. Dumbbell Goblet Squat — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Hold one dumbbell vertically at the chest. Feet slightly wider than hip-width, toes turned out slightly. Inhale at the top, exhale through the ascent. The goblet position encourages an upright torso and makes it easier to manage IAP than a back-loaded squat. Depth is to comfortable range — she does not need to chase full depth yet.

**3. Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Hold both dumbbells in front of the thighs. Hinge at the hips, pushing them back, maintaining a neutral spine. Lower the dumbbells to mid-shin or wherever her hamstring flexibility allows without lumbar rounding. Exhale on the way up. This is the first hinge pattern of the block — watch carefully for any lower back rounding or breath-holding.

**4. Wall Push-Up — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Progressed from Week 1 by adding one rep per set. Same mechanics. If she showed no coning last week, you can begin to move her hands slightly lower on the wall to increase the angle and therefore the load.

**5. Dumbbell Bent-Over Row — 3 sets of 10 reps each side**
Single-arm, supported on a chair or the edge of a sofa. Opposite hand and knee on the surface. Pull the dumbbell from a hanging position to the hip, leading with the elbow. Exhale on the pull. This is the first pulling pattern and will begin to address the postural demands of feeding and carrying.

**6. Dead Bug — 3 sets of 5 reps each side**
Supine, arms pointing to the ceiling, hips and knees at 90 degrees. Slowly lower the opposite arm and leg toward the floor, maintaining the lower back in contact with the floor and breathing continuously. Return and repeat on the other side. This is the primary anti-extension core exercise for the block. If she cannot maintain lumbar contact or holds her breath, regress to arm-only or leg-only movement.

---

### Session B (Day 3 of the week — midpoint)

**1. Clam Shell with Resistance Band — 3 sets of 12 reps each side**
If a band is available, place it just above the knees. Same mechanics as Week 1 but with added resistance. Without a band, add a small dumbbell resting on the outer thigh.

**2. Reverse Lunge — 3 sets of 8 reps each side**
Bodyweight only. Step one foot back and lower the back knee toward the floor. The front shin should remain close to vertical. Exhale on the way up. The reverse lunge is preferred over a forward lunge at this stage because it is easier to control the deceleration forces and reduces pelvic floor loading compared to a forward step. Use a chair for balance support if needed.

**3. Dumbbell Shoulder Press — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Seated on a chair, feet flat on the floor. Press both dumbbells from shoulder height to overhead. Exhale on the press. Watch for rib flare — if the ribs lift aggressively as she presses overhead, cue her to keep the ribcage heavy and connected. This is a common compensation pattern postpartum due to altered thoracic mechanics.

**4. Dumbbell Bicep Curl — 2 sets of 12 reps**
Standing, both dumbbells, alternating or simultaneous. This is included partly for functional carry strength (she is lifting a baby many times a day) and partly because it is accessible and builds confidence with the dumbbells.

**5. Pallof Press Hold — 3 sets of 20-second holds each side**
If she has a resistance band anchored to a door handle or heavy piece of furniture, stand side-on and press the band straight out from the chest, holding for the prescribed time. This is an anti-rotation core exercise and is excellent for rebuilding lateral stability. Without a band, substitute a suitcase carry: hold one dumbbell at the side and walk 10–12 steps, keeping the torso perfectly upright and level. Repeat on the other side.

**6. Hip Flexor Stretch and Thoracic Rotation — 5 minutes**
End Session B with a kneeling hip flexor stretch (30 seconds each side) and a seated or side-lying thoracic rotation (10 reps each side). These address the postural patterns that accumulate from feeding, carrying, and disrupted sleep.

---

### Week 2 Progression Notes
Rest periods should be 60–90 seconds between sets. There is no need to rush. If she is completing all sets and reps with good form and no symptoms, the load is appropriate. If she is breezing through with energy to spare, you can consider increasing the dumbbell weight by the smallest available increment for Week 3 — but do not increase load and volume simultaneously.

---

---

# WEEK 3 — Volume Build

**Goal:** Add a third distinct session structure (previously Sessions A and B were the only templates; now introduce Session C), increase total weekly volume modestly, and begin to challenge single-leg stability more directly.

**Sessions:** 3 sessions | 35–40 minutes each | Full body

---

### Session A (Week 3 version)

**1. Single-Leg Glute Bridge — 3 sets of 8 reps each side**
Progressed from the bilateral loaded bridge. One foot flat on the floor, the other leg extended or held at 90 degrees. This significantly increases the demand on the glute and challenges pelvic stability. If she cannot maintain a level pelvis (watch for the unsupported hip dropping), return to bilateral.

**2. Goblet Squat — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Same as Week 2 but two additional reps per set. If she is comfortable, increase the dumbbell weight slightly.

**3. Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Same progression logic — two additional reps. Focus on tempo: 3 seconds down, 1 second pause at the bottom, drive up.

**4. Incline Push-Up — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Progress from the wall push-up by moving to a kitchen counter, a sturdy table, or the back of a sofa. The lower the surface, the greater the load. Choose a height where she can complete all reps with a rigid torso and no coning.

**5. Dumbbell Bent-Over Row — 3 sets of 12 reps each side**
Two additional reps from Week 2.

**6. Dead Bug — 3 sets of 6 reps each side**
One additional rep per side. Maintain the quality standard — if form degrades, hold at 5.

---

### Session B (Week 3 version)

**1. Reverse Lunge with Dumbbells — 3 sets of 8 reps each side**
Add the dumbbells held at the sides. This is the first time she is combining a single-leg pattern with external load. Start light.

**2. Dumbbell Sumo Squat — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Hold one dumbbell vertically between the legs, feet wider than hip-width, toes turned out significantly. This variation loads the inner thighs and glutes differently from the goblet squat and adds variety to the lower body stimulus.

**3. Dumbbell Shoulder Press — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Two additional reps from Week 2.

**4. Dumbbell Lateral Raise — 2 sets of 12 reps**
Standing, raise both dumbbells to shoulder height with a slight bend in the elbow. Lower with control. This builds shoulder stability and addresses the rounded-shoulder posture common postpartum.

**5. Suitcase Carry — 3 sets of 20 steps each side**
Increased from Week 2. Focus on zero lateral trunk shift.

**6. Side-Lying Hip Abduction — 2 sets of 15 reps each side**
Lying on the side, top leg straight, lift to approximately 45 degrees and lower with control. This targets the glute medius directly and supports pelvic stability during the single-leg work.

---

### Session C (New this week — Day 5 or equivalent)

Session C has a slightly different flavour — it is the lightest session of the week and doubles as active recovery and mobility work, while still including some resistance stimulus.

**1. Breathing and Pelvic Floor — 5 minutes (as per Week 1)**

**2. Cat-Cow into Bird-Dog — 3 sets of 6 reps each side**
From the all-fours position, extend the opposite arm and leg simultaneously, hold for 2 seconds, return. This is a progression of the Week 1 cat-cow and introduces anti-extension and anti-rotation demands simultaneously.

**3. Glute Bridge — 2 sets of 12 reps (bodyweight)**
A deload version of the bridge to maintain the pattern without adding fatigue.

**4. Dumbbell Curl to Press — 2 sets of 10 reps**
Combine the bicep curl and shoulder press into one movement. This adds a small coordination challenge and keeps the session efficient.

**5. Thoracic Extension over a Rolled Towel — 2 minutes**
Place a rolled towel or yoga block under the mid-back (approximately at bra-strap level). Allow the arms to fall overhead and breathe. This is a passive thoracic extension mobilisation and is particularly valuable for the postural demands of new motherhood.

**6. Full Body Stretch — 10 minutes**
Hip flexors, hamstrings, chest opener, side body, and neck. This is not optional — it is part of the session.

---

### Week 3 Nutrition and Recovery Note (if the trainer has asked for this component)
If she is breastfeeding, caloric restriction is contraindicated. She should be eating to support both recovery and milk production. A rough guide is to ensure she is not in a deficit greater than 300–400 kcal below maintenance, and protein intake should be prioritised at approximately 1.6–1.8 g per kg of bodyweight to support tissue repair and muscle adaptation. Encourage her to eat a small protein-containing snack within 30–60 minutes of training. Sleep is the primary recovery tool — if she has had a particularly disrupted night, it is entirely appropriate to skip a session and walk instead.

### End-of-Block Readiness Checklist

Before progressing to a full 12-week programme, you want to be able to answer yes to all of the following:

- She can complete a goblet squat, reverse lunge, Romanian deadlift, push-up, and row with no symptoms (no leaking, no heaviness, no coning, no pain)
- She can coordinate breath with movement consistently across all exercises
- She can maintain a neutral spine under light load in both squat and hinge patterns
- She has no persistent pelvic floor symptoms in the 24 hours following sessions
- Her energy levels are stable enough to support three sessions per week without significant fatigue accumulation
- She has been cleared by her pelvic floor physiotherapist, or you have recommended she see one and she has done so (this is strongly advisable regardless of symptom status)

If she meets all criteria, she is ready for a structured progressive programme. If there are outstanding concerns — particularly around pelvic floor symptoms — extend this on-ramp block by one to two weeks before loading further, and refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist if you have not already done so.

# Cardio Integration — 10 to 14 Weeks Postpartum

## The Honest Conversation First

It is worth having a direct conversation with her about this, because the gap between what she *wants* to do and what her connective tissue and pelvic floor can currently *tolerate* is significant — and that gap is invisible. She will not necessarily feel damage happening in the moment. A former spinner is used to high-intensity, high-cadence work, and her cardiovascular system will recover its fitness relatively quickly. Her pelvic floor and linea alba are on a completely different timeline, and they do not send clear warning signals until the load has already exceeded tolerance.

That said, the desire for cardio is completely valid and you can absolutely honour it. You just need to build the ladder correctly.

---

## What the Tissue Restrictions Actually Mean for Cardio

The OB's no-jumping restriction until 14 weeks covers the most obvious category, but it is worth thinking more broadly about what creates problematic loading at this stage.

**Ground reaction force** is the key variable. Every time a foot strikes the ground, a force travels up through the kinetic chain and is partially absorbed by the pelvic floor. Walking generates roughly 1–1.5 times bodyweight in ground reaction force. Jogging generates 2.5–3 times. Jumping generates 3–5 times or more. Spinning, interestingly, sits in a more nuanced position — the saddle offloads the pelvic floor significantly compared to running, which is one reason it may be appropriate earlier than most people assume. However, standing climbs and high-resistance sprints out of the saddle change that picture considerably.

**Sustained elevated intra-abdominal pressure** is the second concern. Any cardio modality that requires her to brace hard, hold her breath, or generate significant trunk stiffness repeatedly over time will fatigue the pelvic floor in ways that a single strength set does not.

**Hormonal laxity** remains relevant. If she is breastfeeding, relaxin is still circulating. Joints — including the pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joint — are more vulnerable to repetitive stress than they would be in a non-postpartum state.

---

## What Is Safe Right Now, Week by Week

### Weeks 1 and 2 of the Block (10–12 Weeks Postpartum)

**Walking is the primary cardio tool and it is genuinely effective.** This is not a consolation prize — it is the correct prescription. She should be walking daily, and you can structure it progressively rather than leaving it as an afterthought.

Structure her walking like this across the first two weeks:

- **Week 1:** 20–30 minutes at a comfortable conversational pace on non-training days. Flat terrain. She should be able to speak in full sentences throughout. If she notices any pelvic heaviness, pressure, or leaking during or after the walk, shorten the duration and check footwear and posture.
- **Week 2:** Build toward 30–40 minutes. She can begin to introduce gentle inclines if she is symptom-free on flat ground. Inclines increase glute and cardiovascular demand without increasing ground reaction force.

**Cycling (seated, stationary)** is appropriate from Week 1 of this block if she has no perineal tenderness or wound discomfort from the birth. A stationary bike at home or a standard gym bike is fine. The key constraints are:

- Remain seated throughout — no standing climbs yet
- Resistance should be moderate, not high — she should be working at a 5–6 out of 10 perceived effort, not grinding through heavy resistance that causes her to brace hard
- Cadence-based work is preferable to resistance-based work at this stage
- Sessions of 15–20 minutes to begin, building to 25–30 minutes by end of Week 2
- Watch for any saddle pressure discomfort, particularly if she had perineal tearing or stitches

**Swimming** is appropriate from around 10–12 weeks postpartum provided any wounds are fully healed and she has had no signs of infection. The horizontal position and buoyancy offload the pelvic floor almost entirely, making it one of the most pelvic-floor-friendly cardio options available. Breaststroke is the one exception — the frog kick creates significant hip abduction force through the pubic symphysis and should be avoided for now. Front crawl and backstroke are both fine.

---

### Weeks 3 and 4 of the Block (12–14 Weeks Postpartum)

**Walking can now be structured more deliberately.** Introduce interval walking — alternating between a brisk pace (7–7.5 out of 10 effort) and a recovery pace — across 30–40 minute sessions. This begins to approximate the cardiovascular stimulus she is craving without the impact of running.

**Stationary cycling can progress.** She can begin to introduce slightly more resistance and extend sessions to 30–35 minutes. She can experiment with short seated surges — 20–30 seconds of higher cadence or slightly increased resistance — followed by recovery periods. This is essentially a seated spin session and will feel much more familiar to her. Still no standing work yet.

**Low-impact dance or aerobic movement** — if she has access to any low-impact aerobic video content — is appropriate provided there is no jumping, no rapid direction change, and she can maintain breathing throughout. The test is simple: if she has to hold her breath to do it, it is too much right now.

**Rowing machine** is worth considering if she has access to one. It is low-impact, seated, and provides both cardiovascular and upper body stimulus. The catch position (compressed trunk at the front of the stroke) does create some IAP, so she should focus on breathing continuously and not over-compressing. Start with 10–15 minutes at moderate intensity.

---

### At 14 Weeks (End of Block) — The Transition Point

When the OB's jumping restriction lifts, this does not mean she should immediately return to a full spin class. The restriction lifting is a medical clearance, not a fitness readiness assessment. Those are two different things.

**Before she returns to spin**, you want her to pass an informal pelvic floor loading test. The Return to Running guidelines developed by Groom, Donnelly, and Brockwell (widely used by pelvic floor physiotherapists) provide a useful framework even for non-running impact. The key markers are:

- Can she walk briskly for 30 minutes with no symptoms?
- Can she jog on the spot for 1 minute with no symptoms?
- Can she perform 10 single-leg calf raises with no symptoms?
- Can she perform 10 single-leg bridges with no symptoms?
- Is she free of pelvic floor symptoms for at least 24 hours after her current training sessions?

If she passes all of these, a gradual return to spin is reasonable. The first session back should be entirely seated, moderate resistance, 20–25 minutes maximum. She should treat it like Week 1 of the strength block — information gathering, not performance.

---

## How to Integrate Cardio Into the 4-Week Block Practically

Rather than leaving cardio as a separate unstructured activity, weave it into the weekly schedule so it complements the strength sessions rather than competing with them for recovery.

A sample weekly layout might look like this:

**Monday** — Strength Session A
**Tuesday** — 30-minute walk or 20-minute stationary bike (easy)
**Wednesday** — Strength Session B
**Thursday** — 30–40 minute walk, building to interval walk by Week 3
**Friday** — Strength Session C
**Saturday** — 25–30 minute stationary bike (moderate, seated) or swim if available
**Sunday** — Rest or gentle walk only

This gives her six active days, which will feel much more like her pre-pregnancy training rhythm, while keeping the intensity and impact appropriate for where her body actually is.

---

## Managing Her Expectations Around Spin Specifically

She needs to hear this clearly and kindly: **spin will come back, and it will come back relatively soon, but the version she returns to in the first session will not look like the classes she was doing before pregnancy.** Her cardiovascular fitness will return faster than she expects — the heart and lungs adapt quickly. The pelvic floor and connective tissue need more time and more graduated loading.

The worst outcome here is that she rushes back to a full spin class at Week 14, feels fine during it because the adrenaline and music mask any symptoms, and then develops pelvic organ prolapse symptoms or stress incontinence over the following weeks that sets her back by months. The best outcome is that she does the boring work now and is back in a full class — standing climbs included — by Week 8 to 10 of the next programme phase, with a pelvic floor that has been properly prepared for it.

Frame it as building the engine before flooring the accelerator. She would not skip the first four weeks of a spin training block and go straight to race pace. This is the same logic.

---

## One Strong Recommendation

If you have not already, strongly encourage her to see a **pelvic floor physiotherapist** before she returns to any impact work. A single assessment session will give you both objective information about her pelvic floor strength, endurance, and coordination that no amount of symptom monitoring from the outside can provide. It will also give her confidence and a clear green light that is grounded in actual tissue assessment rather than a general OB clearance. This is especially important given her history with high-intensity training — her pelvic floor has more demands ahead of it than the average postpartum client.

# Core Component — Anti-Flexion Focus
### Integrated into the 4-Week On-Ramp Block

## The Programming Philosophy

Before listing exercises, it is worth being precise about terminology because "anti-flexion" can mean different things in different contexts, and at 10 weeks postpartum the distinction matters.

**True anti-flexion** means resisting the spine being pulled into flexion — so the spine wants to round and the task is to prevent that. A Romanian deadlift is anti-flexion. A bird-dog is anti-flexion. A Pallof press has an anti-flexion component. A crunch is the opposite — it is a concentric flexion exercise that shortens the rectus abdominis and dramatically spikes IAP, which is exactly what you do not want at this stage.

However, at 10 weeks postpartum you are also working within a broader framework of **IAP management and load progression**, so the anti-flexion work needs to be layered in carefully. The deep system — transversus abdominis, pelvic floor, diaphragm, multifidus — must be functioning as a unit before you load the outer unit with anti-flexion challenges. The good news is that the breathing work in Week 1 addresses exactly this, so by the time you introduce heavier anti-flexion loading in Weeks 3 and 4, the foundation should be there.

The four anti-flexion categories you will draw from across this block are:

- **Anti-extension** — resisting lumbar extension under load (dead bug, plank progressions, ab wheel)
- **Anti-rotation** — resisting trunk rotation (Pallof press, bird-dog, single-arm carries)
- **Anti-lateral flexion** — resisting side-bending (suitcase carry, side plank progressions)
- **Hip hinge bracing** — maintaining neutral spine under a hinging load (RDL, good morning)

Each week introduces or progresses one or more of these categories. The progression logic is: **position before movement, movement before load, load before speed.**

---

## Core Exercise Library for This Block

The following exercises form the pool you will draw from. Each is described fully here so you have the complete coaching picture, and the weekly integration section below tells you exactly when and how to use each one.

---

### Category 1 — Anti-Extension

**Dead Bug**
Already in the programme. The dead bug is the cornerstone anti-extension exercise for this block because it trains the deep and superficial anterior chain simultaneously while keeping the spine in a safe, supported position. The lumbar spine must remain in contact with the floor throughout — this is the non-negotiable cue. The moment the lower back lifts, the exercise has exceeded her current capacity and needs to be regressed.

*Regression:* Arms only (legs stay at 90/90 and do not move). Or legs only (arms stay pointing to ceiling). Or reduce range of motion on the moving limb.

*Progression pathway across the block:*
- Week 1: Introduce with arm-only or leg-only movement, 5 reps per side
- Week 2: Full contralateral movement, 5–6 reps per side
- Week 3: 7–8 reps per side, focus on slow eccentric (3 seconds lowering)
- Week 4: 8–10 reps per side, add a 2-second pause at full extension before returning

**Hardstyle Plank (Short Duration)**
Not a traditional plank hold — a hardstyle plank is an actively braced, maximally tensioned position held for 10 seconds at a time rather than endured for minutes. She squeezes everything — glutes, quads, lats pulling the elbows toward the feet — and breathes shallowly but continuously. The short duration means IAP spikes are brief and manageable. This is far more appropriate than a 60-second passive plank hold, which tends to cause breath-holding and pelvic floor fatigue.

*Entry point:* Forearm plank position, 3 sets of 3 × 10-second efforts with 5 seconds rest between efforts. Total plank time per set is 30 seconds but it is broken into active chunks.

*Prerequisite:* She should not attempt this until Week 3 at the earliest, and only if the dead bug has been symptom-free for two weeks. If she shows any coning in the plank position, return to dead bug only.

*Regression:* Elevated forearm plank with hands on a counter or step — reduces the load significantly and makes it easier to maintain position.

**Ab Wheel Rollout (Kneeling, Short Range)**
This is a Week 4 exercise only, and only if she has been symptom-free throughout the block. The kneeling rollout is one of the most effective anti-extension exercises available but it is also one of the most demanding on the linea alba. Short range means rolling out only to the point where she can maintain a neutral spine and continuous breathing — for most postpartum clients this is 30–40% of the full range initially. If she does not have an ab wheel, a dumbbell on a hard floor works as a substitute.

*Prerequisite:* Symptom-free hardstyle plank in Week 3, no coning observed in any exercise across the block.

---

### Category 2 — Anti-Rotation

**Bird-Dog**
Already introduced in Week 3 as a progression of cat-cow. The bird-dog is simultaneously anti-extension and anti-rotation, making it exceptionally efficient for this block. The coaching focus is on the pelvis — it must not rotate as the leg extends. Place a water bottle on her lower back as a feedback tool if you are training in person; it should not fall off during the movement.

*Progression pathway:*
- Week 3: Standard bird-dog, 6 reps per side, 2-second hold at extension
- Week 4: Add a slow elbow-to-knee crunch at the midpoint (bringing the extended arm and leg to meet under the body before re-extending) — this adds a brief anti-extension demand at the midpoint and increases the coordination challenge without adding load

**Pallof Press**
Already in the programme as a hold. The Pallof press deserves more detailed coaching notes because it is often performed incorrectly in ways that reduce its effectiveness.

She should stand side-on to the anchor point with feet hip-width apart, slight knee bend, and a tall spine. The band or cable should be at chest height. She holds the handle at her sternum, braces gently (exhale to set the brace, then breathe normally), and presses straight out from the chest. The rotational pull of the band is the stimulus — her job is to prevent any trunk rotation. She should feel this in the obliques and deep stabilisers, not the shoulders.

*Common errors:* Holding the breath throughout, allowing the hips to shift toward the anchor, pressing at an angle rather than straight out.

*Progression pathway:*
- Week 2: Isometric hold, 20 seconds per side
- Week 3: Press and hold — press out, hold 3 seconds, return. 8 reps per side
- Week 4: Press, hold, and add a slow march — while holding the press, lift one knee to hip height and lower. 6 reps per side. This adds a significant anti-rotation and anti-lateral flexion demand simultaneously

**Single-Arm Dumbbell Press (Standing or Seated)**
Any unilateral pressing or pulling exercise has an anti-rotation component because the asymmetric load tries to rotate the trunk. The single-arm overhead press and single-arm row are already in the programme — flag these to her as core exercises, not just shoulder or back exercises. The core demand is real and she should feel it if she is bracing correctly.

---

### Category 3 — Anti-Lateral Flexion

**Suitcase Carry**
Already in the programme. This is one of the most underrated core exercises available and is particularly relevant for a new mother who is carrying a baby on one hip for hours every day. The task is simple — hold a dumbbell in one hand and walk without allowing the trunk to lean toward the weight. The obliques on the opposite side are working hard to prevent lateral flexion.

*Progression pathway:*
- Week 2: 10–12 steps per side, light dumbbell
- Week 3: 20 steps per side, moderate dumbbell
- Week 4: 25–30 steps per side, or increase the dumbbell weight

*Coaching cue:* Imagine a glass of water balanced on the top of her head. Not a drop should spill.

**Side Plank Progression**
The side plank is the primary anti-lateral flexion exercise and it has a clear progression ladder that maps well onto this four-week block.

*Week 2 entry point — Side-Lying Hip Lift (Bent Knee):*
Lying on her side, knees bent, hips stacked. She lifts the hips off the floor so the body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Hold for 5–8 seconds, lower, repeat 5 times. This is a very accessible entry point that most postpartum clients can manage without symptoms.

*Week 3 progression — Side Plank from Knees:*
Same position but feet stacked or staggered rather than knees bent. The lever arm is longer and the demand is greater. Hold for 10 seconds, 3–4 times per side. Breathing must remain continuous.

*Week 4 progression — Side Plank from Feet (Short Hold):*
Full side plank from the feet, held for 10 seconds at a time. Same hardstyle approach as the front plank — 3 × 10 seconds per side rather than one long hold. If she cannot maintain a straight body line from feet to shoulders without the hips sagging or the top hip rotating forward, stay at the knee version.

*Watch for:* Hip dropping (insufficient lateral strength), top hip rotating forward (compensation from hip flexors), breath-holding.

---

### Category 4 — Hip Hinge Bracing

**Romanian Deadlift (Core Framing)**
The RDL is already in the programme as a lower body exercise. Reframe it explicitly as a core exercise when you coach it. The anti-flexion demand — maintaining a neutral spine while the hamstrings pull the pelvis into posterior tilt and gravity pulls the weight toward the floor — is substantial. The erectors, multifidus, and deep stabilisers are all working hard throughout the movement.

*Coaching cue for the core component:* Before she hinges, cue her to take a breath in, brace gently (not a maximal Valsalva — think 30–40% of maximum brace), and maintain that brace throughout the descent. Exhale at the top. This is the same bracing strategy she will use in any loaded hinge for the rest of her training life.

**Good Morning (Bodyweight)**
Introduce this in Week 3 as a complement to the RDL. Standing, hands behind the head or crossed at the chest, she hinges at the hips with a slight knee bend until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor, then returns to standing. No load initially — the bodyweight lever of the torso is sufficient. This reinforces the hinge pattern and the anti-flexion bracing demand without the additional variable of holding dumbbells.

*Progression:* In Week 4, she can hold a light dumbbell at the chest to add a small amount of load.

The core work should not be bolted on at the end of sessions as an afterthought. Some of it belongs in the warm-up (breathing, dead bug), some of it is embedded in the main exercises (RDL, single-arm row, carries), and some of it forms a dedicated core block of 8–10 minutes within the session.

Diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor connection — 10 breath cycles. This is the foundation of everything else. Without this, the anti-flexion work has no base to build on.

Dead bug — arm-only variation, 2 sets of 5 reps per side. Focus entirely on keeping the lower back flat and breathing continuously. This is assessment as much as training.

**Daily homework:**
5 minutes of breathing practice. This is not optional — it is the most important core work she does this week.

**What you are looking for:**
Can she maintain lumbar contact with the floor during the dead bug? Does she hold her breath? Does she show any coning? The answers determine how you load Week 2.

## A Note on Cueing Language

The way you cue core engagement matters enormously at this stage. Avoid cues like *"brace hard," "pull your belly button to your spine,"* or *"tighten your core."* These tend to produce either a breath-hold or a downward bearing-down pressure on the pelvic floor — neither of which you want.

More useful cues:

- *"Breathe in to prepare, breathe out and feel the ribcage soften down"*
- *"Imagine you are fogging up a mirror — that gentle exhale is your brace"*
- *"Keep the breath moving — if you are holding your breath, the weight is too heavy or the range is too much"*
- *"Long spine — think about creating space between each vertebra"*
- *"Resist the pull — don't let it win"* (for Pallof press and carries)

The goal is a **responsive, coordinated core** — not a rigid, braced one. She is building a system that can manage load dynamically, which is exactly what she needs for the demands of motherhood and eventually for returning to spin.

# Diastasis Recti Screening Protocol
### For Use Across the 4-Week On-Ramp Block and Beyond

## Important Framing First

Before getting into the practical protocol, there are two things worth being clear about — one for you as the trainer, and one that you should communicate directly to your client.

**For you:** Screening for diastasis recti (DR) as a personal trainer sits at the edge of your scope of practice. You are not diagnosing. You are not treating. What you are doing is observing, gathering information, and making programming decisions based on what you find — and referring appropriately when the picture is unclear or concerning. The gold standard assessment for DR is an ultrasound performed by a pelvic floor physiotherapist or women's health physiotherapist. Nothing you do in a home setting replaces that, and if there is any doubt at any point, the referral conversation needs to happen. With that clearly established, there is a meaningful and appropriate role for a trainer in monitoring DR across a programme, and doing it well makes a real difference to client outcomes.

**For her:** She needs to understand what diastasis recti actually is, because the term gets thrown around in postpartum fitness spaces with a lot of fear attached to it that is not always warranted. A separation of the linea alba is present in virtually all women at term pregnancy — it is a normal adaptation to accommodate the growing uterus. The question is not whether a separation exists but whether the tissue has sufficient **tension and load transfer capacity** to support her training and daily life. A gap measurement alone tells you very little. A 2 cm gap with good tension is functionally better than a 1.5 cm gap with poor tension. This distinction matters enormously for how you both interpret what you find.

---

## What You Are Actually Assessing

There are three variables that matter in a DR screen, and gap width is only one of them.

**1. Inter-Recti Distance (IRD) — the gap**
The distance between the medial borders of the two rectus abdominis muscles at the linea alba. Measured in finger widths in a clinical setting, or in centimetres with ultrasound. The commonly cited threshold of 2 finger widths or 2 cm as the definition of DR is somewhat arbitrary and increasingly questioned in the research literature, but it remains a useful clinical reference point. More important than the number is whether the gap changes meaningfully under load.

**2. Tissue Tension — the quality of the gap**
When you palpate the linea alba, does the tissue feel firm and springy under your fingers, or does it feel soft, empty, and unsupportive? Good tension means the connective tissue is doing its job of transferring load across the midline even if a gap is present. Poor tension means load transfer is compromised regardless of gap size. This is the variable that most directly affects her training capacity.

**3. Functional Load Transfer — what happens under task**
Does the midline hold its integrity when she performs a movement? Coning or doming — where the midline bulges upward in a ridge or cone shape — indicates that IAP is exceeding the tissue's ability to manage it. This is the most practically relevant variable for a trainer because you can observe it in real time during exercise.

---

## The Self-Check Protocol — Teaching Her to Monitor Herself

Because you are not with her every day and because DR monitoring is most useful when it is ongoing rather than periodic, the most valuable thing you can do is teach her to perform a reliable self-check. This gives her body awareness, removes fear by replacing it with information, and means she is gathering data between your sessions.

Walk her through this in Week 1, ideally in your first session together. It takes about five minutes and she can repeat it weekly at home.

---

### Step-by-Step Self-Check

**Position:** Lie on her back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor. This is the same semi-supine position she uses for breathing work, so it should already feel familiar.

**Step 1 — Locate the landmarks**
Ask her to find her navel with one hand and her pubic bone with the other. The linea alba runs vertically between these two points. She will be checking at three locations: just above the navel (approximately 2–3 cm), at the navel, and just below the navel (approximately 2–3 cm). These three points give a more complete picture than checking at one location only, because the separation can vary significantly along the length of the linea alba.

**Step 2 — The resting check**
With her head resting on the floor and her body completely relaxed, she places two fingers horizontally across the midline at the first check point (above the navel). She presses gently — not hard — into the tissue. She is feeling for the edges of the rectus abdominis muscles on either side and noting how many finger widths fit between them. She repeats at the navel and below the navel. She notes the numbers.

**Step 3 — The loaded check**
She keeps her fingers in place at whichever location showed the widest gap in the resting check. She then performs a very small head lift — just enough to bring her chin toward her chest, not a full crunch. This is the minimum load needed to create tension in the anterior abdominal wall. As she lifts, she notes two things: does the gap narrow (good — the tissue is responding to load), stay the same, or widen (concerning)? And does the tissue under her fingers feel firm and supportive, or does it feel like her fingers are sinking into an unsupported space?

**Step 4 — The tension assessment**
With her fingers resting in the gap at the loaded position, she gently tries to press her fingers deeper into the tissue. If the tissue resists — if it feels like pressing against a trampoline — tension is present. If her fingers sink easily with little resistance, tension is poor. This is subjective but with practice she will develop a reliable sense of the difference.

**Step 5 — Record and report**
She notes the widest gap in finger widths, the location of the widest gap, whether the gap narrowed or widened under load, and her subjective sense of tissue tension. She reports this to you at each session.

---

### What the Numbers Mean in Practice

Give her this simple framework so she knows how to interpret what she finds without catastrophising:

**Gap of 1 finger width or less with good tension:** No functional concern. Train normally within the programme parameters.

**Gap of 1–2 finger widths with good tension:** Within normal range for this stage postpartum. Continue programme as planned. Monitor weekly.

**Gap of 2–3 finger widths with good tension:** Proceed with the programme but be conservative with loading. Avoid any exercise that produces coning. Refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for a formal assessment within the next two to four weeks.

**Gap of any width with poor tension:** This is the more significant finding. Reduce loading, avoid any exercise that increases IAP significantly, and refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist promptly. This does not mean stopping all exercise — walking, breathing work, and gentle pelvic floor work are all still appropriate — but it does mean pausing the strength and core progression until she has been formally assessed.

**Gap that widens under load:** Refer regardless of the resting measurement. A gap that widens under load suggests the tissue is not managing the demand and needs professional assessment before further loading.

---

## Your In-Session Observation Protocol

In addition to the self-check she performs at home, you should be actively screening for DR indicators during every training session. This does not require touching her — it is entirely observational.

### The Visual Coning Check

At the start of each new exercise and whenever you increase load, watch the midline. Ask her to lift her shirt or wear a crop top during sessions so you can see the abdominal wall clearly. You are looking for:

**Coning:** A ridge or cone shape that rises along the midline, most visible between the navel and the sternum. This indicates that IAP is exceeding the tissue's load management capacity at that moment. It is your immediate signal to regress — reduce the load, modify the breathing strategy, or change the exercise.

**Doming:** A broader, more diffuse bulging of the entire midline rather than a sharp ridge. Similar significance to coning — the tissue is not managing the load.

**Asymmetry:** One side of the abdomen appearing to work harder than the other, or the navel being pulled to one side during movement. This can indicate uneven tension through the linea alba and is worth noting even if coning is not present.

Check for coning specifically during:
- The concentric phase of the goblet squat (standing up from the bottom)
- The top of the glute bridge
- The pressing phase of the push-up
- The lowering phase of the dead bug
- Any overhead pressing movement
- The hinge in the Romanian deadlift

### The Breathing Observation Check

Breath-holding is a proxy indicator for excessive IAP. If she is holding her breath during any exercise, the load is either too heavy or the movement is too complex for her current capacity. Watch for:
- Visible breath-holding (no chest or ribcage movement during the effort phase)
- Reddening of the face
- Audible straining
- Pursed lips or clenched jaw

Any of these means the exercise needs to be modified immediately.

### The Post-Session Symptom Check

At the end of every session, ask her directly: any leaking, any pelvic heaviness or pressure, any pain at the midline or pubic symphysis, any unusual fatigue in the abdominal area? These questions should become routine — not alarming, just informational. If she reports any of these symptoms consistently after sessions, the programme needs to be reviewed and a physiotherapy referral made.

---

## Formal Check-In Points Across the Block

Rather than leaving monitoring entirely to ongoing observation, build three formal check-in points into the block where you specifically review the DR picture together.

### Check-In 1 — End of Week 1

This is the baseline. She performs the self-check protocol and reports to you. You observe her during the wall push-up and chair squat for any coning. You are establishing the starting point, not making any judgements about whether she can train. Record the findings.

Questions to ask:
- What is the widest gap and where is it located?
- Does the gap narrow or widen under the head lift load?
- How does the tissue tension feel — firm or soft?
- Any symptoms during or after this week's sessions?

### Check-In 2 — End of Week 2

Compare to baseline. Has the gap changed? Has tension improved? Are there any symptoms emerging now that she is under light load? This check-in is particularly important because Week 2 introduces the first meaningful resistance training. If the tissue is responding poorly to even light loading, you need to know now before Week 3 increases the volume.

Questions to ask:
- Same gap measurement questions as Week 1
- Any coning observed during the goblet squat, RDL, or push-up?
- Any symptoms during or after sessions?
- How does the tissue feel compared to last week — any change in tension?

### Check-In 3 — End of Week 4

This is the end-of-block assessment. You are making a decision about readiness to progress. The DR picture is one component of that decision alongside the pelvic floor symptom picture and the movement quality assessment described in the main programme document.

Questions to ask:
- All previous questions
- Has the gap been consistently stable or improving across the block?
- Has she been symptom-free for the last two weeks of training?
- Is tissue tension good across all three check points?
- Has any coning been observed in the last two weeks?

If the answers are positive across the board, she is ready to progress with appropriate monitoring continuing into the next phase. If there are outstanding concerns, extend the on-ramp block and refer for formal assessment.

---

## Red Flags That Require Immediate Referral

The following findings at any point in the block should prompt you to pause the programme and refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist or women's health physiotherapist without waiting for the next scheduled check-in:

- A gap that is widening over successive weeks rather than staying stable or narrowing
- Consistent coning during exercises that should be well within her capacity
- Any pain at the midline, particularly a sharp or pulling sensation
- A palpable soft spot or depression at the linea alba that she can feel with her fingers at rest — this may indicate a hernia and requires medical review, not just physiotherapy
- Persistent pelvic floor symptoms (leaking, heaviness, pressure) that are not resolving between sessions
- Any visible bulging at the navel during rest or light activity
- Her reporting that the gap feels larger or more symptomatic than it did in the previous week

---

## The Referral Conversation

If you need to refer her, frame it carefully. The postpartum fitness space has created a significant amount of anxiety around diastasis recti, and many women have been told they have a serious problem when the reality is more nuanced. Your referral should sound something like this:

*"What I'm seeing is worth getting a proper look at from a specialist. A pelvic floor physiotherapist can do an ultrasound assessment that tells us exactly what the tissue is doing — it's much more precise than what we can do here. It doesn't mean we stop everything, it just means we get better information so I can programme for you more accurately. This is actually a really normal part of postpartum training and the assessment is straightforward."*

The goal is to get her in front of the right professional without creating fear or making her feel like something is badly wrong. In the majority of cases, a pelvic floor physiotherapist will confirm that she can continue training with appropriate modifications — and you will have a much clearer picture of exactly what those modifications should be.

---

## A Note on the Research Landscape

It is worth knowing that the DR research base is evolving quickly and some of the older guidance — particularly around specific gap thresholds and blanket exercise restrictions — is being revised. The current clinical consensus is moving toward **function over measurement**: what matters is whether the tissue can transfer load effectively and whether the client is symptom-free, not whether a gap of a specific width exists. This means that a client with a measurable separation who is training symptom-free with good tissue tension and no coning is in a better position than the gap number alone would suggest. Keep this in mind when interpreting what you find and when talking to her about it — the number is context, not a verdict.

# Managing the "Feeling Great" Moment
### A Framework for Intensity Progression at 10–12 Weeks Postpartum

## The Most Important Thing to Say First

This moment — where she feels great and wants to push — is one of the most critical decision points in the entire postpartum return-to-training process, and it is genuinely good news that she feels this way. But it is also the moment where the most setbacks happen, and understanding why will help you hold the line intelligently rather than just telling her no.

The reason this moment is deceptive is neurological and hormonal before it is structural. Her cardiovascular system, her nervous system, and her mood-regulating hormones are recovering faster than her connective tissue. She feels good because her energy systems are coming back online. Her linea alba, her pelvic floor fascia, and her relaxin-affected ligaments are on a completely different recovery curve — slower, less perceptible, and silent until they are overloaded. The feeling of readiness is real. It is just not a reliable indicator of tissue readiness.

There is also a specific postpartum phenomenon worth naming: many women have a window of elevated energy around weeks 10–14 postpartum that does not necessarily reflect their overall recovery trajectory. Sleep deprivation tends to be somewhat more manageable by this point, the acute physical recovery from birth is largely complete, and the hormonal picture is stabilising. This window can feel like a green light when it is actually more of an amber.

None of this means you ignore how she feels. It means you use it strategically.

---

## The Distinction Between Intensity and Load

Before deciding what to change, it is worth being precise about what "pushing intensity" actually means, because different types of intensity carry very different risk profiles at this stage.

**Cardiovascular intensity** — working harder aerobically — is the safest lever to pull right now. Her heart and lungs can handle more than her connective tissue can. Increasing the effort level of her walks, extending her stationary bike sessions, or adding more structured intervals to her cardio work is a reasonable response to feeling great with a relatively low downside risk.

**Mechanical load** — adding weight to exercises — is a moderate-risk lever. It is appropriate to progress, but it needs to be done incrementally and with close symptom monitoring. Adding 1–2 kg to a goblet squat is very different from jumping to a significantly heavier dumbbell.

**Volume** — adding sets or reps — is also moderate risk. More total work means more cumulative IAP exposure and more fatigue, which can unmask pelvic floor symptoms that do not appear in shorter sessions.

**Movement complexity** — progressing to harder exercise variations — carries the highest risk of the four because it changes the biomechanical demand in ways that are harder to predict and monitor. Moving from a reverse lunge to a forward lunge, or from a wall push-up to a floor push-up, changes the load on the pelvic floor and linea alba in ways that are not simply linear.

The safest response to feeling great in Week 2 is to pull the cardiovascular intensity lever first, the mechanical load lever second and conservatively, and to leave movement complexity progression on the Week 3 schedule where it already belongs.

---

## What You Should and Should Not Change Mid-Week 2

### Reasonable to Progress Now

**Cardio duration and structure**
If she has been doing 20–25 minute walks, move to 30–35 minutes. If she has been doing 15–20 minutes on the stationary bike, extend to 25 minutes and introduce two or three short seated surges — 30 seconds at a higher cadence, then 90 seconds recovery. This will feel much more like the training she is used to and is a legitimate intensity increase with minimal tissue risk.

**Rest periods**
Shortening rest periods from 90 seconds to 60 seconds between sets increases cardiovascular demand and metabolic stress without changing the mechanical load on the tissue at all. This is an underused progression tool in postpartum training and is appropriate here.

**Tempo**
Adding a slower eccentric phase to exercises she is already performing well increases time under tension and therefore training stimulus without adding load. A goblet squat with a 3-second descent is meaningfully harder than the same squat performed at a normal tempo. A Romanian deadlift with a 4-second lowering phase will challenge her hamstrings and posterior chain more than the current version. This is a high-quality progression that also tends to improve movement mechanics.

**Dumbbell weight — selective and small**
If she is completing all sets and reps of the bent-over row and Romanian deadlift with clearly no effort in the final reps, a 1–2 kg increase is appropriate. These two exercises are the most appropriate candidates for a small load increase at this stage because they are hinge and pull patterns where she has the most structural support. Do not increase load on the goblet squat yet — the squat pattern under load is where coning is most likely to appear, and you want more weeks of data before adding weight there.

---

### Not Appropriate to Change Yet

**Exercise selection**
The exercises in Week 2 are there for a reason. The reverse lunge, goblet squat, and push-up progressions are scheduled for Week 3 because they represent a meaningful step up in demand. Moving them into Week 2 because she feels good compresses the progression timeline in a way that removes the buffer you have built in for tissue adaptation. Feeling great in Week 2 does not mean the tissue has adapted — it means the nervous system has. Those are different things.

**Core exercise progression**
The dead bug, side plank, and Pallof press progressions are on a specific schedule tied to tissue readiness, not perceived effort. Do not advance these ahead of schedule. The core is the area where overconfidence causes the most lasting setbacks.

**Session frequency**
Three sessions per week is the correct frequency for this stage. Adding a fourth session because she feels good increases cumulative fatigue and reduces the recovery time that connective tissue needs. If she has energy to spare, direct it toward the cardio work and the daily walking rather than adding a strength session.

**Any impact work**
She is still two weeks away from the OB's jumping clearance. This does not move regardless of how she feels.

---

## A Practical Mid-Week 2 Session Adjustment

If you want to give her something concrete that reflects her progress without compromising the programme integrity, here is how you might adjust a single Session B in Week 2:

Take the existing session and make the following changes only:

Reduce rest periods to 60 seconds throughout. Add a 3-second eccentric to the Romanian deadlift and the reverse lunge. Increase the bent-over row by the smallest available dumbbell increment. Extend the suitcase carry from 12 steps to 16 steps per side. Add one additional set of the Pallof press hold.

That is a meaningfully harder session than the original Week 2 Session B. It will feel like a real workout. And it has not changed a single exercise, introduced any new movement complexity, or pushed into territory that the tissue is not ready for.

---

## How to Have This Conversation With Her

She needs to hear that her progress is real and that you are responding to it — not that you are ignoring how she feels in favour of a rigid plan. The framing matters.

Something like this works well:

*"The fact that you feel this good at Week 2 is genuinely a great sign — it means your cardiovascular system and nervous system are recovering well and that the programme is pitched at the right level. What I want to do is use that energy in the right places. We can push the cardio harder right now — that's where your body is ready for more. On the strength side, I'm going to add some tempo work and tighten the rest periods, which will make the sessions feel harder without changing the exercises. The reason I'm not jumping ahead on the exercise progressions is that the tissue underneath — the connective tissue and pelvic floor — adapts on a slower timeline than how you feel, and it doesn't give you warning signals until it's already been overloaded. We're two weeks away from the progressions I already have planned. Let's earn those rather than borrow against them."*

Most clients respond well to this framing because it acknowledges their progress, gives them something to look forward to, and explains the reasoning without being dismissive.

---

## The Monitoring Obligation That Comes With Any Progression

If you do make any of the adjustments described above, you take on an increased monitoring obligation for the remainder of Week 2 and the start of Week 3. Specifically:

Ask her to perform the DR self-check the morning after the first adjusted session and report back. Ask directly about pelvic floor symptoms — not just during sessions but in the 24 hours following. Watch more carefully for coning during the exercises where you have increased tempo or load. If anything changes in the symptom picture, dial back immediately and return to the original Week 2 parameters.

The adjusted session is a test as much as a workout. Treat the data it generates accordingly.

---

## The Bigger Picture

Her feeling great at Week 2 is information about where this programme is going, not a reason to change where it is right now. The most valuable thing you can do with that energy is channel it into building the habit of consistent training, the cardio base that will support her return to spin, and the movement quality that will make the Week 3 and Week 4 progressions feel strong rather than effortful.

The clients who make the best long-term progress after having a baby are almost never the ones who pushed hardest in the early weeks. They are the ones who built the foundation carefully enough that nothing broke, and who arrived at the more demanding phases of training with their tissue integrity intact and their confidence high.

She is on track for that. The job right now is to keep her there.

# HIIT Integration for Fat Loss
### Postpartum-Appropriate Programming Within the On-Ramp Block

## The Conversation You Need to Have Before Programming Anything

This request needs a direct, honest response before it needs a programme. Not because HIIT is off the table — it is not, and she will get back to it — but because the specific combination of **HIIT, fat loss, and early postpartum** carries enough nuance that programming without addressing it first would be doing her a disservice.

### On Fat Loss Specifically

Fat loss as an explicit goal at 10–12 weeks postpartum needs to be handled carefully, and the reason is physiological rather than aesthetic or judgemental.

If she is breastfeeding, she is already in a mild caloric deficit relative to her total energy demands in many cases, and her body is actively prioritising milk production over other metabolic processes. Deliberately adding a significant energy deficit on top of this can reduce milk supply, increase cortisol, impair connective tissue healing, and paradoxically make fat loss harder by elevating stress hormones that promote fat retention — particularly around the abdomen. The research on this is reasonably consistent: aggressive caloric restriction while breastfeeding is counterproductive on multiple fronts.

If she is not breastfeeding, the picture is somewhat different, but the connective tissue healing argument still applies. Tissue repair requires adequate protein and caloric availability. A significant deficit at this stage slows the very healing process that determines how quickly she can progress her training.

The most honest thing you can tell her is that the best fat loss strategy available to her right now is building lean muscle through the strength programme, managing cortisol through adequate recovery, and eating to support healing. The body composition changes will follow. Chasing fat loss aggressively at 12 weeks postpartum tends to extend the timeline rather than shorten it.

That said — she wants HIIT, it was important to her pre-pregnancy, and there is a version of it that is appropriate right now. Your job is to give her that version while being transparent about what it is and what it is not.

### On HIIT and the Pelvic Floor

High-intensity interval training in its traditional form — burpees, jump squats, box jumps, high knees, sprint intervals — is not appropriate at this stage. The ground reaction forces, the sustained elevated IAP, and the breath management demands of true HIIT exceed what her tissue can reliably handle at 10–12 weeks postpartum. This is not a permanent restriction. It is a current one.

What is appropriate is **metabolic conditioning work** — training that elevates heart rate significantly, creates a meaningful cardiovascular and metabolic stimulus, and produces the hormonal environment associated with fat loss, without the impact loading and IAP spikes of traditional HIIT. This is not a consolation prize version of HIIT. Done correctly, it is highly effective training. But you should call it what it is rather than labelling it HIIT and having her feel like she is getting something she is not.

At 14 weeks postpartum — the end of this block — a genuine return-to-impact assessment can happen, and if she passes it, low-impact HIIT with progressive reintroduction of jumping movements becomes appropriate. That is the goal to work toward.

---

## What the Research Actually Says About HIIT and Fat Loss

It is worth knowing this so you can speak to it confidently with her.

The fat loss advantage of HIIT over moderate-intensity continuous training is real but more modest than popular fitness culture suggests. The primary mechanisms are excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC), improved insulin sensitivity, and favourable hormonal responses — particularly growth hormone and catecholamines. However, EPOC from a typical HIIT session adds perhaps 50–150 additional calories of expenditure over the following hours. The bigger driver of body composition change is the muscle mass built through resistance training, which elevates resting metabolic rate continuously rather than transiently.

The practical implication for her programme is that the strength work she is already doing is doing more for her long-term body composition than any amount of HIIT would at this stage. The metabolic conditioning you are about to add will accelerate the process and give her the intensity she is craving. But the foundation is the lifting.

---

## The Progressive HIIT Return Framework

Structure the return to HIIT across three stages that map onto the current block and the programme that follows it.

---

### Stage 1 — Metabolic Conditioning (Weeks 2–4 of the On-Ramp Block)
*No impact. No jumping. Elevated heart rate through resistance-based circuits and cardio intervals.*

### Stage 2 — Low-Impact HIIT (Weeks 1–4 of the next programme phase, approximately 14–18 weeks postpartum)
*Impact reintroduced progressively. Jumping movements added one at a time after passing the readiness screen.*

### Stage 3 — Full HIIT (From approximately 18–20 weeks postpartum onward, subject to symptom status)
*Traditional HIIT formats reintroduced. Spin classes with standing work. Plyometric training.*

This document covers Stage 1 in full and outlines Stage 2 so you have the roadmap.

---

---

# STAGE 1 — Metabolic Conditioning Circuits
### Weeks 2–4 of the On-Ramp Block

## Programming Structure

Metabolic conditioning sessions replace one of the existing cardio sessions per week — they do not add to the total training volume. The weekly schedule therefore looks like this:

**Monday** — Strength Session A
**Tuesday** — Walk or easy bike (30 minutes)
**Wednesday** — Strength Session B
**Thursday** — Metabolic Conditioning Session
**Friday** — Strength Session C
**Saturday** — Walk or easy bike (30–35 minutes)
**Sunday** — Rest

The metabolic conditioning session sits on Thursday because it is maximally separated from the strength sessions, giving her the best chance of recovering adequately from both stimuli. If her schedule requires a different placement, the principle is simply to avoid putting it the day before or after a strength session if possible.

---

## Session Structure for All Metabolic Conditioning Sessions

Every session follows the same architecture:

**Warm-up — 5 minutes**
Not optional and not rushed. Her heart rate needs to be elevated gradually, her joints need to be prepared, and her pelvic floor needs to be primed. Use the breathing protocol from the main programme followed by 2 minutes of brisk walking on the spot with arm swings, hip circles, and bodyweight squats.

**Work Block — 16–20 minutes**
Circuit-based. Work-to-rest ratios are prescribed below and progress across the weeks. All exercises are low-impact and chosen for their metabolic demand relative to their IAP and ground reaction force profile.

**Cool-Down — 5 minutes**
Breathing reset (4–5 cycles), full body stretch, pelvic floor symptom check.

**Total session time:** 26–30 minutes.

---

## Exercise Pool for Metabolic Conditioning

The following exercises form the library for all Stage 1 circuits. Each is selected because it generates meaningful cardiovascular demand without jumping, without sustained breath-holding, and without excessive IAP.

**Lower Body**

*Step Touch* — A lateral step-touch pattern, arms moving in opposition. Simple, effective, elevates heart rate quickly. The entry-level option for any circuit.

*Lateral Step Squat* — Step to the side, squat, step back to centre, repeat on the other side. Adds a squat stimulus to the step touch pattern.

*Reverse Lunge with Knee Drive* — From the reverse lunge position, drive the back knee toward the chest as she stands. No jumping — the foot stays in contact with or close to the floor. This is the closest she gets to a high-knee movement at this stage and is surprisingly cardiovascular.

*Squat to Calf Raise* — Squat down, stand, rise onto the toes. The calf raise at the top adds a small cardiovascular spike and challenges balance.

*Lateral Band Walk* — If she has a resistance band, place it above the knees and walk laterally for the prescribed duration. Glute medius dominant, low IAP, moderate cardiovascular demand.

*Glute Bridge March* — In the bridge position, alternately lift each foot off the floor in a slow marching pattern. Maintains glute activation while adding a coordination and stability challenge.

**Upper Body**

*Dumbbell Thruster (Light)* — A goblet squat into a shoulder press in one fluid movement. This is the highest-demand exercise in the pool and should only be introduced in Week 4 when she has demonstrated good form in both component movements. Use the lightest available dumbbell.

*Dumbbell Curl to Press* — Already in the programme. Included here as a circuit exercise because the continuous movement elevates heart rate more than the same exercises performed with full rest between sets.

*Bent-Over Dumbbell Row (Bilateral)* — Both dumbbells simultaneously, hinged position. More cardiovascular than the single-arm supported version because of the sustained hinge position.

*Dumbbell Lateral Raise to Front Raise* — Alternating lateral and front raises continuously for the prescribed duration. Shoulder endurance and cardiovascular demand without any spinal loading.

**Full Body**

*Bear Crawl (Short Distance)* — On all fours, knees hovering 2–3 cm off the floor, crawl forward 4–5 steps and back. Surprisingly demanding cardiovascularly, excellent anti-extension core stimulus, zero impact. Watch for breath-holding.

*Mountain Climber (Slow)* — In a push-up position, slowly alternate driving each knee toward the chest. The key word is slow — this is not the fast version. Slow mountain climbers allow continuous breathing and manageable IAP while still being cardiovascularly effective. If she shows any coning in the plank position, remove this exercise.

*Dumbbell Deadlift to Upright Row* — Romanian deadlift, then as she stands, pull the dumbbells up to chin height with elbows leading. A full posterior chain and upper back movement that creates significant metabolic demand.

*Farmer Carry (Fast Walk)* — Both dumbbells held at the sides, walking as briskly as possible for the prescribed distance or time. The bilateral version of the suitcase carry with a cardiovascular emphasis.

---

## Week-by-Week Metabolic Conditioning Sessions

---

### Week 2 — Introduction Session

**Format:** 3 rounds of a 5-exercise circuit
**Work interval:** 30 seconds per exercise
**Rest between exercises:** 30 seconds
**Rest between rounds:** 90 seconds
**Total work block time:** Approximately 16 minutes
**Target heart rate:** 65–75% of maximum (she should be breathing harder than a walk but able to speak in short phrases)

**Circuit:**
1. Lateral Step Squat — 30 seconds
2. Reverse Lunge with Knee Drive (right leg) — 30 seconds
3. Reverse Lunge with Knee Drive (left leg) — 30 seconds
4. Dumbbell Curl to Press — 30 seconds
5. Bear Crawl — 30 seconds

*Rest 90 seconds. Repeat for 3 rounds.*

**Coaching notes for this session:**
This is her first taste of structured metabolic work since before pregnancy. The 30:30 work-to-rest ratio is conservative by design — she will almost certainly feel like she could do more. That is correct. The purpose of this session is to establish that she can perform circuit-style training without symptoms, not to maximise the training stimulus. Watch carefully for coning during the bear crawl and the reverse lunge. Ask about pelvic floor symptoms immediately after the session and the following morning.

If she reports any symptoms, the next metabolic session should use a 20:40 work-to-rest ratio and remove the bear crawl.

---

### Week 3 — Building Session

**Format:** 4 rounds of a 5-exercise circuit
**Work interval:** 35 seconds per exercise
**Rest between exercises:** 25 seconds
**Rest between rounds:** 75 seconds
**Total work block time:** Approximately 20 minutes
**Target heart rate:** 70–80% of maximum

**Circuit:**
1. Lateral Step Squat — 35 seconds
2. Reverse Lunge with Knee Drive (alternating) — 35 seconds
3. Bent-Over Dumbbell Row (bilateral) — 35 seconds
4. Slow Mountain Climber — 35 seconds
5. Farmer Carry (fast walk, 10 metres and back) — 35 seconds

*Rest 75 seconds. Repeat for 4 rounds.*

**Coaching notes for this session:**
The work interval has increased by 5 seconds, the rest between exercises has decreased by 5 seconds, and there is now a fourth round. This is a meaningful step up from Week 2. The alternating reverse lunge with knee drive is more demanding than the single-leg version because there is no rest between sides. The slow mountain climber is introduced here — watch the midline carefully in the first round and remove it immediately if coning appears.

The farmer carry at the end of each circuit serves as active recovery relative to the other exercises while still maintaining heart rate. It also reinforces the anti-lateral flexion core work from the main programme.

**Variation option:** If she found Week 2 very easy and is clearly ready for more, you can add a sixth exercise to this circuit — the Squat to Calf Raise — and keep the same work-to-rest ratio. Do not increase both the circuit length and the work interval simultaneously.

---

**Format:** 4 rounds of a 6-exercise circuit
**Work interval:** 40 seconds per exercise
**Rest between exercises:** 20 seconds
**Rest between rounds:** 60 seconds
**Total work block time:** Approximately 22 minutes
**Target heart rate:** 75–85% of maximum

**Circuit:**
1. Lateral Step Squat — 40 seconds
2. Reverse Lunge with Knee Drive (alternating) — 40 seconds
3. Dumbbell Thruster (light) — 40 seconds
4. Slow Mountain Climber — 40 seconds
5. Dumbbell Deadlift to Upright Row — 40 seconds
6. Farmer Carry (fast walk) — 40 seconds

*Rest 60 seconds. Repeat for 4 rounds.*

**Coaching notes for this session:**

It is the most demanding exercise in the pool and combines the goblet squat and shoulder press patterns she has been building across the block. Use the lightest available dumbbell — the cardiovascular demand of the circuit context means even a very light weight will feel challenging. Watch for coning at the top of the press and breath-holding during the squat phase.

The 40:20 work-to-rest ratio is approaching the territory of traditional HIIT protocols. She should be working hard during the work intervals and using the rest periods genuinely. If she is chatting comfortably during the rest periods, the work intervals were not hard enough.

By the end of this session she should have a clear sense of what her body can handle at intensity. This information directly informs the Stage 2 programming.
