## Monitoring Protocol Specific to Metabolic Conditioning

The monitoring obligations for these sessions are higher than for the strength sessions because the cumulative IAP exposure across a circuit is greater than in a single-exercise set. Apply the following checks:

**During the session:**
Watch for coning on every exercise in the first round. If it appears on any exercise, remove that exercise for the remainder of the session and note it for modification next week. Watch for breath-holding — in a circuit context this is more likely because she is working harder and the rest periods are shorter. If she is consistently holding her breath, the work interval is too long or the exercise is too demanding.

**Immediately after the session:**
Ask directly about leaking, heaviness, pelvic pressure, and midline discomfort. These questions should be asked within five minutes of finishing, not at the end of the cool-down, because symptoms can appear quickly and then fade.

**The following morning:**
Ask her to check in via message. Delayed onset pelvic floor symptoms — heaviness or pressure that appears the day after training rather than during it — are a significant indicator that the session exceeded her tissue's recovery capacity. If this happens, reduce the work interval by 10 seconds and increase the rest by 10 seconds for the following session.

# STAGE 2 — Low-Impact HIIT Roadmap
### Approximately Weeks 1–4 of the Next Programme Phase (14–18 Weeks Postpartum)

This section gives you the roadmap for what comes next so you can brief her on it now. Knowing there is a clear pathway back to real HIIT will make the Stage 1 constraints easier to accept.

## The Readiness Screen Before Starting Stage 2

Before introducing any impact work, she needs to pass the following screen. This should be performed at the end of Week 4 of the on-ramp block.

**Single-leg calf raise test:** 20 consecutive single-leg calf raises on each side with no symptoms. This tests the load tolerance of the foot, ankle, and calf complex that will absorb ground reaction force during impact.

**Jog on the spot test:** 1 minute of jogging on the spot at a comfortable pace with no symptoms — no leaking, no heaviness, no pelvic pressure. If she cannot pass this test, impact work is not yet appropriate regardless of how she feels during training.

**Single-leg balance:** 10 seconds of single-leg balance on each side with eyes open, then eyes closed. This tests the proprioceptive readiness that impact training demands.

**Hop test:** 10 single-leg hops on each side — small, low hops — with no symptoms. This is the final gate before returning to jumping movements.

If she passes all four, Stage 2 can begin. If she fails any one of them, extend Stage 1 by two weeks and retest.

## Stage 2 Exercise Progression

The principle in Stage 2 is to reintroduce impact one movement at a time, starting with the lowest ground reaction force and progressing upward. The order is:

**Week 1 of Stage 2:** Introduce double-leg skipping (with a rope or imaginary rope) — 20 seconds on, 40 seconds off. This is the lowest-impact jumping movement available. Monitor for symptoms.

**Week 2:** Add squat jumps — landing softly with knees bent, absorbing the landing over 2–3 seconds. 15 seconds on, 45 seconds off initially.

**Week 3:** Add alternating split jumps (lunge jumps) — 15 seconds on, 45 seconds off.

**Week 4:** Introduce a full low-impact HIIT circuit combining the above with the Stage 1 exercises. Work-to-rest ratio of 30:30, building toward 40:20 across the phase.

By the end of Stage 2 she will be performing genuine HIIT with impact work included, and the pathway back to spin classes with standing climbs will be open.

---

## The Fat Loss Conversation — Revisited

Now that the programming is in place, it is worth returning to the fat loss goal with something concrete to offer her.

The combination of three strength sessions, one metabolic conditioning session, and three to four cardio sessions per week that this programme now represents is a genuinely effective body composition programme. The strength work builds and preserves lean mass. The metabolic conditioning creates the EPOC and hormonal environment she associates with HIIT. The cardio work manages overall energy expenditure. And the progressive nature of the block means the stimulus is increasing week on week.

What will accelerate the fat loss results more than any additional training is the nutrition picture. If she is not already doing so, encourage her to:

Prioritise protein at every meal — 1.6–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight daily. Protein has the highest thermic effect of any macronutrient, supports muscle retention during any deficit, and manages satiety better than carbohydrate or fat.

Avoid a deficit greater than 300–400 kcal below maintenance if breastfeeding, or 400–500 kcal if not. Larger deficits at this stage impair recovery and connective tissue healing in ways that extend the overall timeline.

Time carbohydrate intake around training sessions — a moderate carbohydrate meal or snack in the two hours before training and within 45 minutes after will support performance and recovery without compromising fat loss.

Prioritise sleep above all else. Cortisol from sleep deprivation is the single biggest obstacle to fat loss in the postpartum period. No training programme overcomes chronically elevated cortisol. On nights where sleep has been severely disrupted, replacing the metabolic conditioning session with a walk is the correct call — not a failure of discipline, but an intelligent physiological decision.

The body composition results she wants are coming. The programme she is on is building toward them correctly. The worst thing that could happen right now is that she pushes too hard, develops a pelvic floor issue that sidelines her for six to eight weeks, and loses all the momentum she has built. The best thing is that she arrives at Stage 2 with her tissue intact, her fitness base rebuilt, and a clear runway back to the training she loves.

# Return to Running Programme
### Postpartum Pathway to a 10k Autumn Goal

## Setting the Scene — What We Know

Before building the timeline, it is worth consolidating what we know about where she is and what the autumn goal requires.

She is currently 10–12 weeks postpartum and in Week 2 of a 4-week on-ramp block. Assuming autumn means September or October, and assuming we are currently in late spring or early summer, she has approximately 16–24 weeks from the end of the on-ramp block to a 10k event. That is a workable timeline — not generous, but workable — provided the return to running is managed correctly from the start and nothing significant interrupts the progression.

The 10k goal is actually a useful motivational anchor for the entire programme. It gives the strength work, the metabolic conditioning, and the pelvic floor rehabilitation a clear purpose beyond general fitness. Everything you are building now is infrastructure for that goal.

---

## The Honest Timeline

The most commonly cited clinical guideline for return to running postpartum — drawn from the Groom, Donnelly, and Brockwell framework that has become the standard reference for pelvic floor physiotherapists — is **a minimum of 12 weeks postpartum** before any running, with the emphasis on minimum. The guideline is not 12 weeks and you are ready. It is 12 weeks and you can begin assessing readiness.

She is already at 10–12 weeks. So the timeline from here looks like this:

**Weeks 10–14 postpartum (current on-ramp block):** No running. Build the foundation. Pass the readiness screen.

**Weeks 14–18 postpartum (Stage 2 of the next phase):** Impact reintroduction begins. Jogging on the spot, short run-walk intervals. This is where running starts, not where it becomes a training tool.

**Weeks 18–22 postpartum:** Graduated run-walk programme. Building toward continuous running of 20–30 minutes.

**Weeks 22–28 postpartum:** Continuous running established. Begin structured 10k-specific training.

**Weeks 28–32+ postpartum:** 10k race-ready, depending on her progression through each phase.

If autumn is 24 weeks away from now, this timeline is tight but achievable. If it is closer to 20 weeks, you need to have a conversation about whether the goal is the 10k distance or the 10k race — because completing a run-walk version of a 10k event is a different target from racing one, and the former is more realistic on a compressed timeline.

---

## Why Running Is More Demanding Than People Assume

She needs to understand why running cannot simply be slotted in as cardio once she feels fit enough, because the gap between her current fitness and running readiness is not cardiovascular — it is structural.

Running generates ground reaction forces of approximately 2.5 times bodyweight with every foot strike. At an easy pace of around 9–10 minutes per kilometre, a 10k involves roughly 9,000–10,000 foot strikes. Each one sends a force wave up through the kinetic chain that the pelvic floor must absorb and manage. The pelvic floor is functioning as a shock absorber, a pressure management system, and a dynamic stabiliser simultaneously — and it is doing this thousands of times per run.

At 12–14 weeks postpartum, the pelvic floor has been through significant trauma regardless of delivery method. Vaginal delivery creates direct mechanical stress on the pelvic floor muscles and fascia. Caesarean delivery removes that specific stress but involves abdominal wall trauma that affects the entire pressure management system. In both cases, the tissue is still healing and its load tolerance is significantly below pre-pregnancy levels — even if she feels completely normal.

The additional factor is that running requires single-leg stance for approximately 60% of the gait cycle. Every time she is on one leg, the entire pelvis is being supported by the hip abductors, glute medius, and pelvic floor on that side. If any of these are not functioning optimally — and at 12 weeks postpartum they almost certainly are not — the compensations that develop can create injury patterns that persist long after the postpartum period ends.

This is not a reason to avoid running. It is a reason to build toward it correctly.

---

## The Readiness Screen — Gate One

Before any running begins, she needs to pass a two-part readiness screen. The first part is the physical screen you can administer. The second part is a pelvic floor physiotherapy assessment, which is non-negotiable before she starts a running programme.

### Physical Readiness Screen
*(To be performed at the end of the on-ramp block, approximately 14 weeks postpartum)*

Administer all of the following. She must pass every single item — this is not a majority vote situation. One failure means the running programme does not start until that item is addressed.

**Walking base:** She can walk briskly for 30 minutes on varied terrain with no pelvic floor symptoms during or in the 24 hours following. This should already be established by the end of the on-ramp block.

**Single-leg calf raise:** 20 consecutive single-leg calf raises on each side with no symptoms and no significant asymmetry between sides. The calf complex is the primary shock absorber for running and needs to be strong and resilient.

**Single-leg balance:** 10 seconds eyes open, 10 seconds eyes closed on each side. Running requires sophisticated proprioception and balance that a bilateral training programme does not fully develop.

**Single-leg squat:** 10 controlled single-leg squats on each side to approximately 60 degrees of knee flexion, with no knee cave, no trunk sway, and no pelvic drop. This tests the hip and glute strength that running demands.

**Jog on the spot:** 1 minute at a comfortable pace with no symptoms. This is the minimum impact test before progressing to forward running.

**Forward running test:** 200 metres at an easy pace on a flat surface. Stop and assess immediately — any leaking, heaviness, pelvic pressure, or pain means she is not ready. Assess again 30 minutes later and the following morning for delayed symptoms.

**Hop test:** 10 single-leg hops on each side — small, controlled, landing softly. No symptoms.

If she passes all items, proceed to the run-walk programme. If she fails any item, identify the specific weakness, address it in training for two to four weeks, and retest.

### Pelvic Floor Physiotherapy Assessment
*(Strongly recommended before starting the run-walk programme)*

A pelvic floor physiotherapist can assess internal muscle strength, endurance, coordination, and relaxation capacity in ways that no external screen can replicate. For a client with a 10k goal, this assessment is particularly valuable because it will identify any specific deficits that need to be addressed before the running load accumulates.

If she has not seen a pelvic floor physiotherapist by the end of the on-ramp block, make this a condition of starting the run-walk programme. Frame it as getting the green light from the right professional rather than as a barrier to her goal.

---

## The Run-Walk Programme
### Approximately Weeks 14–22 Postpartum

The run-walk programme is the bridge between no running and continuous running. It is not a beginner running programme in the traditional sense — it is a tissue loading programme that uses running as the stimulus. The distinction matters because it changes how you think about progression. You are not trying to build cardiovascular fitness here. You are trying to progressively load the pelvic floor, the connective tissue, and the musculoskeletal system with running-specific forces while monitoring the response carefully.

### General Principles

**Every session starts with a 5-minute brisk walk.** This is not optional warm-up padding. The transition from walking to running involves a significant increase in ground reaction force, and the pelvic floor needs to be primed and activated before that transition happens.

**Running intervals are always on flat, even surfaces initially.** Hills increase ground reaction force and pelvic floor demand. They come later.

**Cadence matters more than pace.** A higher cadence — more steps per minute — reduces ground reaction force per step compared to a slower, longer stride. Aim for approximately 170–180 steps per minute during running intervals. This will feel faster and shorter than her natural stride but is significantly more pelvic-floor-friendly. A metronome app on her phone can help establish this.

**The two-hour rule.** She should be completely symptom-free for two hours after every run-walk session before progressing. Any symptoms within that window mean the session was too much and the next session should be regressed.

**The 10% rule applies but conservatively.** Traditional running programmes use a 10% weekly mileage increase. For postpartum return to running, treat this as a ceiling rather than a target. Some weeks the increase will be less than 10% and that is correct.

**She should not run on consecutive days** during the run-walk phase. The tissue needs 48 hours between running sessions to adapt. Running on consecutive days during this phase is the single most common cause of setbacks.

---

### Phase 1 — Run-Walk Introduction
*(Weeks 14–16 postpartum, assuming she passes the readiness screen)*

**Frequency:** 2 sessions per week, non-consecutive days
**Session duration:** 20–25 minutes total including warm-up walk

**Week 14–15:**
5-minute brisk walk warm-up. Then: 1 minute running, 2 minutes walking. Repeat 6 times. 5-minute cool-down walk. Total running time: 6 minutes.

The 1:2 run-to-walk ratio is deliberately conservative. Six minutes of total running in a session sounds trivial to a former spinner who used to do HIIT. It is not trivial for her pelvic floor at 14 weeks postpartum. Monitor symptoms rigorously after every session.

**Week 16:**
If Week 14–15 sessions were completely symptom-free: 1.5 minutes running, 2 minutes walking. Repeat 6 times. Total running time: 9 minutes.

If any symptoms appeared in Week 14–15: Stay at 1:2 ratio for another week before progressing.

---

### Phase 2 — Building Running Intervals
*(Weeks 16–20 postpartum)*

**Frequency:** 2–3 sessions per week
**Session duration:** 25–30 minutes total

Progress the run-walk ratio across this phase as follows, moving to the next step only when the current step has been completed symptom-free for two consecutive sessions:

**Step 1:** 2 minutes running, 2 minutes walking × 6. Total running: 12 minutes.

**Step 2:** 3 minutes running, 2 minutes walking × 5. Total running: 15 minutes.

**Step 3:** 4 minutes running, 2 minutes walking × 4. Total running: 16 minutes.

**Step 4:** 5 minutes running, 2 minutes walking × 4. Total running: 20 minutes.

**Step 5:** 8 minutes running, 2 minutes walking × 3. Total running: 24 minutes.

Do not rush through these steps. A client who takes four weeks to move from Step 1 to Step 5 and arrives at continuous running with no symptoms is in a far better position than one who rushes through in two weeks and develops stress incontinence or pelvic organ prolapse symptoms that require a six-week break to resolve.

---

### Phase 3 — Continuous Running Established
*(Approximately Weeks 20–24 postpartum)*

**Frequency:** 3 sessions per week
**Target by end of phase:** 30 minutes of continuous running at an easy, conversational pace

**Week 20–21:**
20 minutes continuous running. This is the first time she runs without a walk break. The psychological shift here is significant — acknowledge it. Monitor symptoms carefully because the cumulative pelvic floor load of 20 minutes of continuous running is substantially greater than anything she has done in the run-walk phase.

**Week 22:**
25 minutes continuous running.

**Week 23:**
30 minutes continuous running.

Once she can run 30 minutes continuously and symptom-free on three occasions, she has established a running base and is ready for structured 10k training.

---

## The 10k Training Block
### Approximately Weeks 24–32+ Postpartum

With a running base established, the 10k training block can begin. The structure below assumes she has approximately 8–10 weeks between establishing her running base and the target race. If the timeline is tighter, the priority is completing the distance rather than optimising performance.

### Weekly Structure

The 10k training block runs alongside a modified version of the strength programme — not instead of it. Strength training is what keeps her injury-free during the running build. Removing it to make room for more running is a false economy.

**Weekly template:**

**Monday:** Strength session (lower body and core focus)
**Tuesday:** Easy run — 30–35 minutes at conversational pace
**Wednesday:** Strength session (upper body and core focus)
**Thursday:** Tempo or interval run (see below)
**Friday:** Rest or easy walk
**Saturday:** Long run (see below)
**Sunday:** Rest

**Three types of run sessions:**

*Easy runs* are the foundation. She should be able to hold a full conversation throughout. These build aerobic base, promote recovery, and accumulate the running-specific tissue adaptation she needs. Approximately 70% of all running volume should be at this effort level.

*Tempo runs* introduce sustained moderate-to-hard effort — approximately 7–8 out of 10 perceived exertion — held for a defined period. Start with 10 minutes at tempo effort within a 25-minute run (5-minute easy warm-up, 10-minute tempo, 10-minute easy cool-down). Build the tempo segment by 2 minutes per week up to 20 minutes.

*Long runs* build the endurance base specifically for the 10k distance. Start at 35 minutes and build by approximately 5 minutes per week. The long run should always be at easy pace — this is not the place to push effort.

### 8-Week 10k Build

| Week | Easy Run | Tempo Run | Long Run | Total Running Time |
|------|----------|-----------|----------|--------------------|
| 1 | 30 min | 10 min tempo in 25 min | 35 min | ~90 min |
| 2 | 32 min | 12 min tempo in 27 min | 38 min | ~97 min |
| 3 | 35 min | 14 min tempo in 29 min | 42 min | ~106 min |
| 4 | 30 min | 10 min tempo in 25 min | 35 min | ~90 min — deload |
| 5 | 35 min | 16 min tempo in 31 min | 45 min | ~111 min |
| 6 | 38 min | 18 min tempo in 33 min | 50 min | ~121 min |
| 7 | 35 min | 20 min tempo in 35 min | 55 min | ~125 min |
| 8 | 25 min easy | 15 min tempo in 25 min | Race week | Taper |

Week 4 is a deliberate deload — volume drops by approximately 15% to allow tissue adaptation to consolidate before the second half of the build. This is not optional. Skipping the deload week is one of the most common causes of injury in the final weeks before a race.

By Week 7 she will have run 55 minutes continuously at easy pace. A 10k at easy-to-moderate effort will take her approximately 55–70 minutes depending on her fitness level. The long run in Week 7 therefore represents a meaningful simulation of the race demand.

---

## Strength Training Modifications During the Running Build

As running volume increases, the strength programme needs to adapt to avoid cumulative fatigue becoming a problem. The key modifications are:

**Reduce lower body strength volume by approximately 20–25% once the long run exceeds 40 minutes.** The legs are accumulating significant training stress from the running and do not need the same strength volume they required in the on-ramp phase. Maintain the movement patterns but reduce sets from 4 to 3 and consider reducing load slightly on the heaviest lower body exercises.

**Maintain upper body and core volume.** Running does not stress the upper body meaningfully, so there is no reason to reduce this work. A strong upper body and well-functioning core are actually protective against running injuries.

**Prioritise single-leg strength work.** The reverse lunge, single-leg Romanian deadlift, and single-leg glute bridge are more specific to running than bilateral exercises. As the programme evolves, shift the balance of lower body work toward unilateral exercises.

**Add calf and foot strength work.** The calf complex absorbs the majority of running-related ground reaction force and is frequently undertrained in general fitness programmes. Add standing calf raises — progressing to single-leg — and toe-spreading exercises to every strength session from the point that running begins.

---

## Red Flags That Require Stopping and Reassessing

At any point in the return-to-running process, the following symptoms require her to stop running and seek assessment from a pelvic floor physiotherapist before continuing:

Any urinary leaking during or after running, even a small amount. Leaking is not normal and is not something to train through. It is a signal that the pelvic floor load is exceeding its current capacity.

Any sensation of heaviness, pressure, or bulging in the pelvic floor during or after running. This may indicate pelvic organ prolapse and requires prompt assessment.

Any pain at the pubic symphysis or sacroiliac joint. These joints are still vulnerable to stress-related injury while relaxin is present, particularly if she is breastfeeding.

Any pain in the hip, knee, or foot that persists beyond 24 hours after a run. Postpartum ligamentous laxity increases injury risk at these joints and early intervention is far more effective than running through developing injuries.

Persistent fatigue that does not resolve with rest days. This may indicate that the overall training load — running plus strength plus life with a baby — is exceeding her recovery capacity. The correct response is to reduce running volume, not to push through.

---

## The Autumn 10k — A Realistic Picture

If everything goes to plan — she passes the readiness screen at 14 weeks, progresses through the run-walk phases without significant setbacks, and the autumn race is approximately 24 weeks from now — she will arrive at the start line having been running continuously for approximately 8–10 weeks and having completed a structured 10k build.

She will not be in the shape she was pre-pregnancy. Her pace will likely be slower than her pre-pregnancy 10k pace, her legs will fatigue at a different point in the race, and the mental experience of racing on disrupted sleep with a baby at home is genuinely different from racing in a pre-pregnancy context. All of this is normal and temporary.

What she will have is a body that has been prepared correctly for the demand, a pelvic floor that has been loaded progressively rather than shocked, and a training history across the postpartum period that sets her up for years of strong running rather than months of managing the consequences of rushing back too soon.

The 10k is not the destination. It is the first marker on a much longer road. Programme for the road.

# OVERARCHING PRINCIPLES

## Tissue Readiness Versus Perceived Readiness

The most important concept in this entire programme is the gap between how she feels and what her tissue can tolerate. Her cardiovascular system, nervous system, and mood-regulating hormones are recovering faster than her connective tissue. She will feel ready for more before her linea alba, pelvic floor fascia, and relaxin-affected ligaments are ready to deliver it. This gap is invisible and silent until it is exceeded — at which point the consequences can set her back by weeks or months.

Every progression decision in this programme is made with this gap in mind. When she feels great and wants to push — and she will, probably around Week 2 — the response is to pull the cardiovascular intensity lever first, the mechanical load lever second and conservatively, and to leave movement complexity on the schedule where it belongs.

## Symptom Monitoring Is Non-Negotiable

She should be monitoring for the following symptoms during and after every session, and reporting them to you:

- Urinary leaking of any amount
- Heaviness, pressure, or bulging sensation in the pelvic floor
- Coning or doming at the midline during exercise
- Pain at the pubic symphysis, sacroiliac joint, or midline
- Pelvic floor fatigue or discomfort in the 24 hours following a session

Any of these is a signal to regress immediately, not push through. Brief her on this before the first session. Frame it as information gathering rather than alarm — these symptoms are common, they are manageable, and catching them early is far better than ignoring them.

## Intra-Abdominal Pressure Management

Every exercise in this programme is chosen and coached with intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) in mind. The general rule is exhale on the effort — the concentric phase of any movement. Breath-holding during exercise spikes IAP and places excessive demand on the pelvic floor. If she is holding her breath during any exercise, the load is too heavy, the range is too great, or the movement is too complex for her current capacity.

## Cueing Language

Avoid cues that produce breath-holding or downward bearing pressure on the pelvic floor. Specifically avoid: *"brace hard," "pull your belly button to your spine,"* and *"tighten your core."*

Use instead:
- *"Breathe in to prepare, breathe out and feel the ribcage soften down"*
- *"Keep the breath moving — if you are holding your breath, the weight is too heavy"*
- *"Resist the pull — don't let it win"* (for carries and Pallof press)
- *"Long spine — create space between each vertebra"*
- *"Imagine fogging up a mirror — that gentle exhale is your brace"*

## The Fat Loss Context

Fat loss is a stated goal. The honest picture is this: the combination of strength training, metabolic conditioning, and cardio in this programme creates an effective body composition stimulus. The strength work builds lean mass and elevates resting metabolic rate. The metabolic conditioning creates the hormonal environment she associates with HIIT. The cardio manages overall energy expenditure.

What will accelerate results more than any additional training is nutrition. If breastfeeding, she should not be in a caloric deficit greater than 300–400 kcal below maintenance — larger deficits impair milk production, elevate cortisol, and paradoxically slow fat loss. If not breastfeeding, a deficit of 400–500 kcal is appropriate. Protein should be prioritised at 1.6–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight daily to support tissue repair, muscle retention, and satiety. A small protein-containing snack within 30–60 minutes of training supports recovery.

Sleep is the primary recovery tool and the single biggest obstacle to fat loss in the postpartum period. Chronically elevated cortisol from sleep deprivation promotes abdominal fat retention. On nights of severe sleep disruption, replacing a training session with a walk is the correct physiological decision, not a failure of discipline.

## The 10k Context

Everything built in this programme is infrastructure for the autumn 10k goal. The strength work develops the single-leg stability, hip strength, and calf resilience that running demands. The metabolic conditioning rebuilds the cardiovascular base. The progressive loading of the pelvic floor across the block prepares it for the impact demands of running. She will not begin running during this block — the return-to-running programme begins after it — but she will arrive at that starting point significantly better prepared because of the work done here.

# DIASTASIS RECTI SCREENING PROTOCOL

This protocol runs continuously across all four weeks. Read it in full before Week 1 begins.

## What You Are Assessing

Three variables matter. Gap width alone is insufficient.

**Inter-recti distance:** The gap between the medial borders of the rectus abdominis at the linea alba. Measured in finger widths. The commonly cited threshold of 2 finger widths is a reference point, not a verdict — a 2 cm gap with good tension is functionally better than a 1.5 cm gap with poor tension.

**Tissue tension:** Does the linea alba feel firm and springy under load, or soft and unsupportive? Good tension means load transfer is occurring across the midline even if a gap is present.

**Functional load transfer:** Does the midline hold its integrity during movement? Coning or doming — a ridge or cone shape rising along the midline — indicates IAP is exceeding the tissue's management capacity.

## Teaching Her the Self-Check

Walk her through this in the first session of Week 1. She repeats it weekly at home and reports findings to you.

**Position:** Semi-supine, knees bent, feet flat, body relaxed.

**Step 1 — Locate landmarks:** Navel and pubic bone. She will check at three points: 2–3 cm above the navel, at the navel, and 2–3 cm below the navel.

**Step 2 — Resting check:** Two fingers placed horizontally across the midline at each check point. Press gently. Note how many finger widths fit between the muscle edges at each location.

**Step 3 — Loaded check:** Fingers held at the widest gap location. Perform a small head lift — chin toward chest, not a full crunch. Note whether the gap narrows (good), stays the same, or widens (concerning). Note whether the tissue feels firm or soft under the fingers.

**Step 4 — Tension assessment:** With fingers in the gap at the loaded position, gently press deeper. Resistance — like pressing a trampoline — indicates good tension. Fingers sinking easily indicates poor tension.

**Step 5 — Record and report:** Widest gap in finger widths, location, whether it narrowed or widened under load, subjective tension quality.

## Interpreting Findings

**1 finger width or less, good tension:** No functional concern. Train normally.

**1–2 finger widths, good tension:** Normal range for this stage. Continue programme, monitor weekly.

**2–3 finger widths, good tension:** Proceed conservatively. Avoid any exercise producing coning. Refer to pelvic floor physiotherapist within 2–4 weeks.

**Any width, poor tension:** Reduce loading, avoid significant IAP increases, refer promptly. Walking, breathing work, and gentle pelvic floor work remain appropriate.

**Gap widens under load:** Refer regardless of resting measurement.

## Your In-Session Visual Screen

Watch the midline during every new exercise and every load increase. Ask her to wear a crop top or lift her shirt so the abdominal wall is visible.

**Coning:** A ridge rising along the midline — most visible between navel and sternum. Immediate signal to regress.

**Doming:** Broader, more diffuse midline bulging. Same significance as coning.

**Asymmetry:** One side appearing to work harder, or the navel pulling to one side. Note even without coning.

Check specifically during: the concentric phase of the goblet squat, the top of the glute bridge, the pressing phase of push-ups, the lowering phase of the dead bug, all overhead pressing, and the hinge in the Romanian deadlift.

## Formal Check-In Points

# WEEK 1 — ACCLIMATISATION

## Week 1 Overview

**Goal:** Reconnect with her body. Establish breathing mechanics. Assess movement quality. Build the training habit without creating any symptom response. There is no performance target this week. You are gathering information.

**Sessions:** 3 strength sessions, each 20–25 minutes. These are movement conversations, not workouts in the traditional sense.

**Cardio:** Walking only. 20–30 minutes on non-training days, flat terrain, fully conversational pace. If she notices any pelvic heaviness or pressure during walking, shorten the duration and check footwear and posture.

**Core:** Embedded within sessions. Breathing and dead bug only this week.

**DR screen:** Baseline self-check taught and performed at end of Week 1. Record findings.

---

## Session Template — All Three Sessions This Week

All three sessions use the same template intentionally. Repetition at this stage builds motor pattern confidence.

---

### Opening: Diaphragmatic Breathing and Pelvic Floor Reconnection — 5 minutes

Semi-supine position, knees bent, feet flat. One hand on lower ribcage, one on lower abdomen. Breathe into the hands — ribcage expands three-dimensionally on the inhale, softens on the exhale. On the exhale, feel a gentle natural lift and squeeze of the pelvic floor — not a forced Kegel, but a response to the breath. 10 breath cycles. This is also her daily homework performed separately from sessions.

---

### Movement Sequence — 15 minutes

**1. 90/90 Hip Lift — 2 sets of 5 breaths**
Lying supine, feet on a wall or chair at 90 degrees at hip and knee. On the exhale, gently posteriorly tilt the pelvis and feel the lower back connect lightly to the floor. Hold for a breath cycle, release. Resets lumbopelvic position and begins to re-engage deep stabilisers without load.

**2. Glute Bridge — 2 sets of 8 reps**
Supine, feet flat, hip-width apart. Inhale to prepare, exhale and drive through the heels to lift the hips. Cue lengthening the front of the hips rather than squeezing the glutes aggressively. One second hold at the top, lower with control. Watch for rib flare or breath-holding. If pelvic floor heaviness is reported, reduce range of motion.

**3. Clam Shell — 2 sets of 10 reps each side**
Side-lying, hips stacked, knees bent to approximately 45 degrees. Rotate the top knee toward the ceiling, keeping feet together. The pelvis must not rock backward. Slow and controlled throughout.

**4. Cat-Cow — 2 sets of 6 reps**
All fours, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips. Move slowly through spinal flexion and extension, breathing continuously. No breath-holding. Purpose is spinal mobility and body awareness.

**5. Dead Bug — Arm-Only Variation — 2 sets of 5 reps per side**
Supine, arms pointing to ceiling, hips and knees at 90 degrees. Slowly lower one arm toward the floor overhead while the legs remain completely still. Return and repeat on the other side. Lower back must remain in contact with the floor throughout. This is assessment as much as training — watch for lumbar lifting, breath-holding, and any coning.

**6. Wall Push-Up — 2 sets of 8 reps**
Standing facing a wall, hands at shoulder height and width. Inhale lowering toward the wall, exhale pushing away. Watch the midline for coning. This is the first upper body load of the block and the first opportunity to see how her core responds to a pressing pattern.

**7. Chair Squat — 2 sets of 8 reps**
Standing in front of a sturdy chair, feet hip-to-shoulder width. Lower slowly toward the chair — touching lightly or hovering just above — then stand. Exhale on the way up. Watch for knee cave, excessive forward trunk lean, and any pelvic floor symptoms on the ascent.

---

### Cool-Down and Body Awareness — 3–5 minutes

Child's pose (modified with a pillow under the hips if needed), followed by a supine figure-four stretch for the hips. End with 2 minutes back in semi-supine breathing position. Ask her directly: any leaking, heaviness, or discomfort during the session? Any coning noticed? This is data.

## Week 1 Assessment Checklist

By the end of Week 1 you want to know:
- Can she coordinate breath with movement?
- Does she show any symptoms during the bridge, squat, or push-up?
- Does the dead bug produce any coning or lumbar lifting?
- How is her hip mobility and glute activation quality?
- Is she fatigued after 20 minutes or does she have more in the tank?

The answers determine how aggressively you load Week 2.

---

## Week 1 DR Screen

Teach the self-check protocol at the end of the final session of the week. Record baseline findings across all three check points. Note gap width, whether it narrows or widens under load, and tissue tension quality.

# WEEK 2 — FOUNDATION LOADING

## Week 2 Overview

**Goal:** Introduce structured resistance training at low volume. Begin building the squat, hinge, push, pull, and carry patterns that underpin the next phase. Maintain symptom-free training as the non-negotiable standard.

**Sessions:** 3 strength sessions, 30–35 minutes each. Full body each session.

**Cardio:** Walking building to 30–35 minutes on Tuesday. Seated stationary bike introduced Saturday — 20–25 minutes, moderate effort, fully seated, no standing climbs. Cadence-based work preferred over high-resistance grinding.

**Metabolic conditioning:** Not yet introduced. Begins Week 3.

**Core:** Dedicated core block added to Sessions A and B. Dead bug progresses to full contralateral movement. Side-lying hip lift and Pallof press introduced.

**Intensity management:** If she feels great mid-week and wants to push, the appropriate response is: reduce rest periods from 90 to 60 seconds, add a 3-second eccentric to the RDL and reverse lunge, increase the bent-over row by the smallest available dumbbell increment, and extend the suitcase carry from 12 to 16 steps per side. **2. Dumbbell Goblet Squat — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Hold one dumbbell vertically at the chest. Feet slightly wider than hip-width, toes turned out slightly. Inhale at the top, exhale through the ascent. # Complete 4-Week Postpartum Return-to-Fitness Programme
### Fully Integrated — All Components

---

## Client Profile and Programme Context

**Current status:** 10 weeks postpartum
**OB clearance:** Moderate exercise approved. No jumping or high-impact until 14 weeks postpartum (end of Week 4 of this block)
**Training environment:** Home
**Equipment:** Light dumbbells (2–4 kg recommended starting point), resistance band (loop or long, if available), mat, sturdy chair, wall space
**Background:** Former spinner, HIIT enthusiast, strong pre-pregnancy fitness base
**Goals:** Return to fitness, fat loss, 10k in autumn
**Known considerations:** No formal diastasis recti check performed. Pelvic floor status unassessed by physiotherapist. Both of these should be addressed during this block

---

## How to Read This Programme

This document is the single complete reference for the 4-week block. Every component — strength, cardio, metabolic conditioning, core, diastasis screening, and recovery — is integrated into a coherent weekly structure. Nothing is bolted on. Nothing is an afterthought.

Each week has a defined training schedule, full session descriptions, coaching notes, progression logic, and monitoring obligations. Read the overarching principles section before beginning Week 1. They underpin every decision in the programme and will help you coach intelligently when you need to adapt on the fly.

---

---

# OVERARCHING PRINCIPLES

## Tissue Readiness Versus Perceived Readiness

The most important concept in this entire programme is the gap between how she feels and what her tissue can tolerate. Her cardiovascular system, nervous system, and mood-regulating hormones are recovering faster than her connective tissue. She will feel ready for more before her linea alba, pelvic floor fascia, and relaxin-affected ligaments are ready to deliver it. This gap is invisible and silent until it is exceeded — at which point the consequences can set her back by weeks or months.

Every progression decision in this programme is made with this gap in mind. When she feels great and wants to push — and she will, probably around Week 2 — the response is to pull the cardiovascular intensity lever first, the mechanical load lever second and conservatively, and to leave movement complexity on the schedule where it belongs.

## Symptom Monitoring Is Non-Negotiable

She should be monitoring for the following symptoms during and after every session, and reporting them to you:

- Urinary leaking of any amount
- Heaviness, pressure, or bulging sensation in the pelvic floor
- Coning or doming at the midline during exercise
- Pain at the pubic symphysis, sacroiliac joint, or midline
- Pelvic floor fatigue or discomfort in the 24 hours following a session

Any of these is a signal to regress immediately, not push through. Brief her on this before the first session. Frame it as information gathering rather than alarm — these symptoms are common, they are manageable, and catching them early is far better than ignoring them.

## Intra-Abdominal Pressure Management

Every exercise in this programme is chosen and coached with intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) in mind. The general rule is exhale on the effort — the concentric phase of any movement. Breath-holding during exercise spikes IAP and places excessive demand on the pelvic floor. If she is holding her breath during any exercise, the load is too heavy, the range is too great, or the movement is too complex for her current capacity.

## Cueing Language

Avoid cues that produce breath-holding or downward bearing pressure on the pelvic floor. Specifically avoid: *"brace hard," "pull your belly button to your spine,"* and *"tighten your core."*

Use instead:
- *"Breathe in to prepare, breathe out and feel the ribcage soften down"*
- *"Keep the breath moving — if you are holding your breath, the weight is too heavy"*
- *"Resist the pull — don't let it win"* (for carries and Pallof press)
- *"Long spine — create space between each vertebra"*
- *"Imagine fogging up a mirror — that gentle exhale is your brace"*

## The Fat Loss Context

Fat loss is a stated goal. The honest picture is this: the combination of strength training, metabolic conditioning, and cardio in this programme creates an effective body composition stimulus. The strength work builds lean mass and elevates resting metabolic rate. The metabolic conditioning creates the hormonal environment she associates with HIIT. The cardio manages overall energy expenditure.

What will accelerate results more than any additional training is nutrition. If breastfeeding, she should not be in a caloric deficit greater than 300–400 kcal below maintenance — larger deficits impair milk production, elevate cortisol, and paradoxically slow fat loss. If not breastfeeding, a deficit of 400–500 kcal is appropriate. Protein should be prioritised at 1.6–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight daily to support tissue repair, muscle retention, and satiety. A small protein-containing snack within 30–60 minutes of training supports recovery.

Sleep is the primary recovery tool and the single biggest obstacle to fat loss in the postpartum period. Chronically elevated cortisol from sleep deprivation promotes abdominal fat retention. On nights of severe sleep disruption, replacing a training session with a walk is the correct physiological decision, not a failure of discipline.

## The 10k Context

Everything built in this programme is infrastructure for the autumn 10k goal. The strength work develops the single-leg stability, hip strength, and calf resilience that running demands. The metabolic conditioning rebuilds the cardiovascular base. The progressive loading of the pelvic floor across the block prepares it for the impact demands of running. She will not begin running during this block — the return-to-running programme begins after it — but she will arrive at that starting point significantly better prepared because of the work done here.

# DIASTASIS RECTI SCREENING PROTOCOL

This protocol runs continuously across all four weeks. Read it in full before Week 1 begins.

## What You Are Assessing

Three variables matter. Gap width alone is insufficient.

**Inter-recti distance:** The gap between the medial borders of the rectus abdominis at the linea alba. Measured in finger widths. The commonly cited threshold of 2 finger widths is a reference point, not a verdict — a 2 cm gap with good tension is functionally better than a 1.5 cm gap with poor tension.

**Tissue tension:** Does the linea alba feel firm and springy under load, or soft and unsupportive? Good tension means load transfer is occurring across the midline even if a gap is present.

**Functional load transfer:** Does the midline hold its integrity during movement? Coning or doming — a ridge or cone shape rising along the midline — indicates IAP is exceeding the tissue's management capacity.

## Teaching Her the Self-Check

Walk her through this in the first session of Week 1. She repeats it weekly at home and reports findings to you.

**Position:** Semi-supine, knees bent, feet flat, body relaxed.

**Step 1 — Locate landmarks:** Navel and pubic bone. She will check at three points: 2–3 cm above the navel, at the navel, and 2–3 cm below the navel.

**Step 2 — Resting check:** Two fingers placed horizontally across the midline at each check point. Press gently. Note how many finger widths fit between the muscle edges at each location.

**Step 3 — Loaded check:** Fingers held at the widest gap location. Perform a small head lift — chin toward chest, not a full crunch. Note whether the gap narrows (good), stays the same, or widens (concerning). Note whether the tissue feels firm or soft under the fingers.

**Step 4 — Tension assessment:** With fingers in the gap at the loaded position, gently press deeper. Resistance — like pressing a trampoline — indicates good tension. Fingers sinking easily indicates poor tension.

**Step 5 — Record and report:** Widest gap in finger widths, location, whether it narrowed or widened under load, subjective tension quality.

## Interpreting Findings

**1 finger width or less, good tension:** No functional concern. Train normally.

**1–2 finger widths, good tension:** Normal range for this stage. Continue programme, monitor weekly.

**2–3 finger widths, good tension:** Proceed conservatively. Avoid any exercise producing coning. Refer to pelvic floor physiotherapist within 2–4 weeks.

**Any width, poor tension:** Reduce loading, avoid significant IAP increases, refer promptly. Walking, breathing work, and gentle pelvic floor work remain appropriate.

**Gap widens under load:** Refer regardless of resting measurement.

## Your In-Session Visual Screen

Watch the midline during every new exercise and every load increase. Ask her to wear a crop top or lift her shirt so the abdominal wall is visible.

**Coning:** A ridge rising along the midline — most visible between navel and sternum. Immediate signal to regress.

**Doming:** Broader, more diffuse midline bulging. Same significance as coning.

**Asymmetry:** One side appearing to work harder, or the navel pulling to one side. Note even without coning.

Check specifically during: the concentric phase of the goblet squat, the top of the glute bridge, the pressing phase of push-ups, the lowering phase of the dead bug, all overhead pressing, and the hinge in the Romanian deadlift.

## Formal Check-In Points

**End of Week 1:** Baseline. Record all findings. No judgements — information only.

**End of Week 2:** Compare to baseline. Has gap changed? Has tension improved? Any symptoms emerging under light load?

**End of Week 4:** End-of-block assessment. Is the gap stable or improving? Symptom-free for the last two weeks? Good tension across all three check points? No coning in the last two weeks?

## Red Flags Requiring Immediate Referral

- Gap widening over successive weeks
- Consistent coning during exercises well within her capacity
- Pain at the midline, particularly sharp or pulling
- A palpable soft spot or depression at the linea alba at rest — may indicate hernia, requires medical review
- Persistent pelvic floor symptoms not resolving between sessions
- Visible bulging at the navel during rest or light activity

# WEEK 1 — ACCLIMATISATION

## Week 1 Overview

**Goal:** Reconnect with her body. Establish breathing mechanics. Assess movement quality. Build the training habit without creating any symptom response. There is no performance target this week. You are gathering information.

**Sessions:** 3 strength sessions, each 20–25 minutes. These are movement conversations, not workouts in the traditional sense.

**Cardio:** Walking only. 20–30 minutes on non-training days, flat terrain, fully conversational pace. If she notices any pelvic heaviness or pressure during walking, shorten the duration and check footwear and posture.

**Core:** Embedded within sessions. Breathing and dead bug only this week.

**DR screen:** Baseline self-check taught and performed at end of Week 1. Record findings.

---

## Session Template — All Three Sessions This Week

All three sessions use the same template intentionally. Repetition at this stage builds motor pattern confidence.

---

### Opening: Diaphragmatic Breathing and Pelvic Floor Reconnection — 5 minutes

Semi-supine position, knees bent, feet flat. One hand on lower ribcage, one on lower abdomen. Breathe into the hands — ribcage expands three-dimensionally on the inhale, softens on the exhale. On the exhale, feel a gentle natural lift and squeeze of the pelvic floor — not a forced Kegel, but a response to the breath. 10 breath cycles. This is also her daily homework performed separately from sessions.

---

### Movement Sequence — 15 minutes

**1. 90/90 Hip Lift — 2 sets of 5 breaths**
Lying supine, feet on a wall or chair at 90 degrees at hip and knee. On the exhale, gently posteriorly tilt the pelvis and feel the lower back connect lightly to the floor. Hold for a breath cycle, release. Resets lumbopelvic position and begins to re-engage deep stabilisers without load.

**2. Glute Bridge — 2 sets of 8 reps**
Supine, feet flat, hip-width apart. Inhale to prepare, exhale and drive through the heels to lift the hips. Cue lengthening the front of the hips rather than squeezing the glutes aggressively. One second hold at the top, lower with control. Watch for rib flare or breath-holding. If pelvic floor heaviness is reported, reduce range of motion.

**3. Clam Shell — 2 sets of 10 reps each side**
Side-lying, hips stacked, knees bent to approximately 45 degrees. Rotate the top knee toward the ceiling, keeping feet together. The pelvis must not rock backward. Slow and controlled throughout.

**4. Cat-Cow — 2 sets of 6 reps**
All fours, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips. Move slowly through spinal flexion and extension, breathing continuously. No breath-holding. Purpose is spinal mobility and body awareness.

**5. Dead Bug — Arm-Only Variation — 2 sets of 5 reps per side**
Supine, arms pointing to ceiling, hips and knees at 90 degrees. Slowly lower one arm toward the floor overhead while the legs remain completely still. Return and repeat on the other side. Lower back must remain in contact with the floor throughout. This is assessment as much as training — watch for lumbar lifting, breath-holding, and any coning.

**6. Wall Push-Up — 2 sets of 8 reps**
Standing facing a wall, hands at shoulder height and width. Inhale lowering toward the wall, exhale pushing away. Watch the midline for coning. This is the first upper body load of the block and the first opportunity to see how her core responds to a pressing pattern.

**7. Chair Squat — 2 sets of 8 reps**
Standing in front of a sturdy chair, feet hip-to-shoulder width. Lower slowly toward the chair — touching lightly or hovering just above — then stand. Exhale on the way up. Watch for knee cave, excessive forward trunk lean, and any pelvic floor symptoms on the ascent.

---

### Cool-Down and Body Awareness — 3–5 minutes

Child's pose (modified with a pillow under the hips if needed), followed by a supine figure-four stretch for the hips. End with 2 minutes back in semi-supine breathing position. Ask her directly: any leaking, heaviness, or discomfort during the session? Any coning noticed? This is data.

---

## Week 1 Assessment Checklist

By the end of Week 1 you want to know:
- Can she coordinate breath with movement?
- Does she show any symptoms during the bridge, squat, or push-up?
- Does the dead bug produce any coning or lumbar lifting?
- How is her hip mobility and glute activation quality?
- Is she fatigued after 20 minutes or does she have more in the tank?

The answers determine how aggressively you load Week 2.

---

## Week 1 DR Screen

Teach the self-check protocol at the end of the final session of the week. Record baseline findings across all three check points. Note gap width, whether it narrows or widens under load, and tissue tension quality.

# WEEK 2 — FOUNDATION LOADING

## Week 2 Overview

**Goal:** Introduce structured resistance training at low volume. Begin building the squat, hinge, push, pull, and carry patterns that underpin the next phase. Maintain symptom-free training as the non-negotiable standard.

**Sessions:** 3 strength sessions, 30–35 minutes each. Full body each session.

**Cardio:** Walking building to 30–35 minutes on Tuesday. Seated stationary bike introduced Saturday — 20–25 minutes, moderate effort, fully seated, no standing climbs. Cadence-based work preferred over high-resistance grinding.

**Metabolic conditioning:** Not yet introduced. Begins Week 3.

**Core:** Dedicated core block added to Sessions A and B. Dead bug progresses to full contralateral movement. Side-lying hip lift and Pallof press introduced.

**Intensity management:** If she feels great mid-week and wants to push, the appropriate response is: reduce rest periods from 90 to 60 seconds, add a 3-second eccentric to the RDL and reverse lunge, increase the bent-over row by the smallest available dumbbell increment, and extend the suitcase carry from 12 to 16 steps per side. Do not change exercise selection, do not advance core progressions, do not add a fourth session, do not introduce any impact work.

**DR screen:** Second check-in at end of week. Compare to baseline.

---

## Session A — Week 2
*(Monday and repeated Friday with Session C structure — see below)*

### Warm-Up — 5 minutes
8 breath cycles in semi-supine. Then move directly into the session.

### Main Block

**1. Glute Bridge with Dumbbell Hip Load — 3 sets of 10 reps**
Place one light dumbbell across the hip crease. Same mechanics as Week 1 but with external load. If the weight changes her breathing pattern or produces any symptoms, remove the dumbbell and continue unloaded.

**2. Dumbbell Goblet Squat — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Hold one dumbbell vertically at the chest. Feet slightly wider than hip-width, toes turned out slightly. Inhale at the top, exhale through the ascent. The goblet position encourages an upright torso and makes IAP management easier than a back-loaded squat. Depth to comfortable range — no need to chase full depth yet. Watch for coning on the ascent.

**3. Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Hold both dumbbells in front of the thighs. Hinge at the hips, pushing them back, maintaining a neutral spine. Lower to mid-shin or wherever hamstring flexibility allows without lumbar rounding. Exhale on the way up. Cue: inhale at the top, brace gently at 30–40% of maximum — not a Valsalva — maintain through the descent, exhale at the top of the return. This is a core exercise as much as a lower body exercise. Frame it as such.

**4. Wall Push-Up — 3 sets of 10 reps**
One additional rep per set from Week 1. If no coning was observed last week, begin to move the hands slightly lower on the wall to increase the angle and therefore the load.

**5. Dumbbell Bent-Over Row — 3 sets of 10 reps each side**
Single-arm, supported on a chair or sofa edge. Opposite hand and knee on the surface. Pull the dumbbell from hanging to the hip, leading with the elbow. Exhale on the pull. Flag this explicitly as a core exercise — the anti-rotation demand is real and she should feel it in the obliques if bracing correctly.

### Core Block — 8 minutes

**6. Dead Bug (Full Contralateral) — 3 sets of 5 reps each side**
Progress from the arm-only version. Opposite arm and leg lower simultaneously, maintaining lumbar contact with the floor throughout. 3-second lowering phase. If lumbar contact cannot be maintained, regress to arm-only for one more week.

**7. Side-Lying Hip Lift (Bent Knee) — 3 sets of 5 × 8-second holds each side**
Side-lying, knees bent, hips stacked. Lift the hips off the floor so the body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Hold for 8 seconds, lower, repeat 5 times per side. This is the entry-level side plank and the first anti-lateral flexion exercise of the block.

**8. Suitcase Carry — 3 sets of 12 steps each side**
Hold one dumbbell at the side and walk 12 steps, keeping the torso perfectly upright and level. Repeat on the other side. Cue: imagine a glass of water balanced on the top of the head — not a drop should spill.

### Cool-Down — 5 minutes
Hip flexor stretch (30 seconds each side), figure-four stretch, 3 breath cycles to close.

---

## Session B — Week 2
*(Wednesday)*

### Warm-Up — 5 minutes
8 breath cycles. Bodyweight squats × 8, hip circles × 5 each direction.

### Main Block

**1. Clam Shell with Resistance Band — 3 sets of 12 reps each side**
Band placed just above the knees. Same mechanics as Week 1 but with added resistance. Without a band, rest a small dumbbell on the outer thigh.

**2. Reverse Lunge — 3 sets of 8 reps each side**
Bodyweight only. Step one foot back and lower the back knee toward the floor. Front shin remains close to vertical. Exhale on the way up. Use a chair for balance support if needed. The reverse lunge is preferred over a forward lunge at this stage because it reduces pelvic floor loading compared to the forward step deceleration.

**3. Dumbbell Shoulder Press — 3 sets of 8 reps**
Seated on a chair, feet flat on the floor. Press both dumbbells from shoulder height to overhead. Exhale on the press. Watch for rib flare — if the ribs lift aggressively as she presses overhead, cue her to keep the ribcage heavy and connected. This is a common postpartum compensation pattern due to altered thoracic mechanics.

**4. Dumbbell Bicep Curl — 2 sets of 12 reps**
Standing, both dumbbells, alternating or simultaneous. Included for functional carry strength — she is lifting a baby many times daily — and for confidence with the dumbbells.

### Core Block — 8 minutes

**5. Dead Bug (Full Contralateral) — 3 sets of 5 reps each side**
Same as Session A. Consistency of the pattern across sessions is the goal this week.

**6. Pallof Press Hold — 3 sets of 20 seconds each side**
Band anchored to a door handle or heavy furniture at chest height. Stand side-on, feet hip-width, slight knee bend, tall spine. Hold the band at the sternum, brace gently on the exhale, press straight out from the chest and hold. The rotational pull of the band is the stimulus — prevent any trunk rotation. Feel this in the obliques and deep stabilisers, not the shoulders. Without a band, substitute suitcase carry: 3 sets of 12 steps each side.

**7. Side-Lying Hip Abduction — 2 sets of 15 reps each side**
Lying on the side, top leg straight, lift to approximately 45 degrees and lower with control. Targets glute medius directly and supports pelvic stability during single-leg work.

### Cool-Down — 5 minutes
Kneeling hip flexor stretch (30 seconds each side), seated thoracic rotation (10 reps each side), 3 breath cycles.
